blocks.alt: Cory Doctorow speaking in front of shelves of books
blocks.caption: Cory Doctorow introduces malware.

blocks.text: Malware is the collective name for software that has been designed to disrupt or damage data, software or hardware.
blocks.title: Malware

blocks.text: There are several types of malware, such as **viruses**, **worms** and **Trojans**, which you'll learn about in the next few sections.

As malware has evolved from its beginnings as demonstrations of prowess by individual programmers to sophisticated technologies developed by organised crime, the boundaries between the different categories are beginning to blur.
This week you will learn to:

items: describe the different types of malware and their key characteristics
explain how malware gains access to computer systems
take steps to prevent your own computer from being infected

blocks.alt: Magnified spiky virus particles floating in blue
blocks.caption: Figure 1

blocks.text: The best-known type of malware is probably the virus; although many pieces of malware are called viruses, they are nothing of the sort.

A virus is a piece of software that has been written to insert copies of itself into applications and data and onto crucial parts of a computer's data storage systems (e.g. hard disks, memory sticks, etc.).
blocks.title: Virus

blocks.text: Viruses are said to be **self-replicating** programs. They date back as far as the early 1970s, but only became well known with the advent of microcomputers and, later, the internet.

pages.title: How viruses spread and do harm

blocks.text: Viruses attach themselves to specific applications on a computer and are activated when the program is first run. At that point the virus may make a copy of itself on the hard disk and continue to run, or it may only run each time the application is used.

Early viruses relied on floppy disks, spreading quickly as infected disks were shared around an office or pirated software was passed around a playground. Nowadays viruses rely on devices such as flash memory cards or are transmitted through internet connections.

Most viruses are designed to harm users - by corrupting their data, attacking the operating system itself, or providing an exploitable **'back door'** that gives attackers access to the computer. Even where no harm is intended, viruses consume memory, disk space and processing power.

blocks.q: A virus that was written without any intention to cause harm has no effect on the computer it infects.
blocks.explain: Even where no harm is intended, viruses consume memory, disk space and processing power.

blocks.alt: A small worm emerging from a red apple
blocks.caption: Figure 2

blocks.text: Another type of self-replicating malware is the **worm**. Like a virus it is designed to make copies of itself, but unlike a virus, a worm is a **standalone application**.
Worms spread through network connections, accessing uninfected machines and then hijacking their resources to transmit yet more copies across the network.

pages.title: The four stages of a worm attack

items: **Probe** - the worm probes other machines looking for a vulnerability that can be exploited to copy itself to.

**Penetrate** - it performs the operations that exploit the vulnerability; for example, it might detect an open network connection through which it can get the remote machine to execute arbitrary instructions.
**Persist** - the worm downloads itself to the remote machine and stores itself there.
**Propagate** - it picks new machines to attempt to probe.

blocks.text: Worms were invented as a curiosity and have even been suggested as ways of testing networks or distributing software patches, but their drawbacks far outweigh their benefits. Even the most 'benign' worm consumes resources and can affect the performance of a computer system.

blocks.q: In which stage of a worm attack does the worm download itself to the remote machine and store itself there?
options: Probe
Penetrate
Persist
Propagate
blocks.explain: Storing itself on the remote machine is often called the 'persist' stage; propagating comes next, when it picks new machines to probe.

blocks.alt: A wooden Trojan horse being pulled along on a cart
blocks.caption: Figure 3

blocks.text: The final major type of malware is the **Trojan** (or Trojan horse), named after the wooden horse that supposedly smuggled Greek soldiers into the ancient city of Troy.

A Trojan disguises itself as an entirely legitimate program (such as a screensaver), but behind the scenes it is causing damage - perhaps allowing someone else to gain control of the computer, copying personal information, deleting information, monitoring keystrokes, or using email software to pass itself on to other computers.
blocks.title: Trojan

blocks.text: Unlike viruses and worms, Trojans are **not self-replicating** - they rely on their apparent usefulness to spread between computers.

Some Trojans work in isolation. Others rely on networks, either to transmit stolen information - such as passwords, bank account details or credit card numbers - or to act as **back doors** to compromised computers. They allow attackers to bypass the operating system's security features and gain access to data or even control the machine over a network.
Trojans have become a serious problem with Android apps.

blocks.q: What mainly distinguishes a Trojan from viruses and worms?
options: It only attacks Android phones
It is not self-replicating and spreads by appearing useful
It spreads only over network connections
It never damages data
blocks.explain: Viruses and worms copy themselves; a Trojan relies on its apparent usefulness to persuade people to install and pass it on.

blocks.alt: A person typing on a laptop resting on a pile of books
blocks.caption: Figure 4

blocks.text: Besides viruses, worms and Trojans, you may have heard of other kinds of malware:

items: **Adware** - forces users to view advertising.
**Spyware** - malware that attempts to access personal information and user passwords.

blocks.title: Match each type of malware to its description

pairs.def: Inserts copies of itself into applications and data; activated when the infected program runs
A standalone self-replicating program that spreads through network connections
Disguises itself as a legitimate program and is not self-replicating
Forces users to view advertising
Attempts to access personal information and user passwords

blocks.title: Define a malware term in your own words
blocks.prompt: Look through the Sophos Threatsaurus A-Z (downloaded in Week 1) for a term that you have not come across before. Write a definition of the term in your own words. You could also look at examples or information from the sources recommended in Week 1, Section 2.2 'How to keep up to date'.
blocks.model: Answers will vary with the term chosen. A good definition says what kind of threat it is (e.g. a type of malware or an attack technique), how it gets onto or affects a system, and what harm it can cause - for example, 'Ransomware is malware that locks or encrypts your files and demands payment to release them.' Checking the term against a second source helps confirm your understanding.
points: Names the type of threat or malware
Explains how it works or spreads
Describes the harm or purpose
Uses your own words, checked against a reliable source

pages.title: 2 How malware gets into your computer

blocks.alt: Abstract image of a laptop surrounded by floating spheres of numbers
blocks.caption: Figure 5

blocks.text: Malware can get into a computer through a variety of mechanisms, most of which involve exploiting a combination of **human and technical factors**.

For example, a malware creator might get you to download their malware by putting a link in an email, or by attaching the malware to an email. Alternatively, malware might be packaged with **illegal copies of standard software**, so that it gets into the machines of people who use these copies rather than paying for genuine versions.
Before looking at how malware gets in, it's worth asking why it does: what is malware for?

blocks.alt: A city at night with curved lines connecting different parts
blocks.caption: Figure 6

blocks.text: There are many reasons why malware is created, including **intellectual curiosity**, **financial gain** or **corporate espionage**.

Many programmers thrive on the challenge of seeing what is possible, and create malware even if they do not intend harm. Perhaps the most famous of these experiments was the **1988 Morris Worm** - the first worm to spread over the internet. Its supposed intent was to gauge the number of machines connected to the network, but it slowed infected machines to the point of being unusable.
Worms continue to represent a major threat, as the Conficker Worm of 2008 showed.
In 2008, Microsoft Windows computers began being infected by an advanced worm called **Conficker**, which spread when users shared files, either over networks or via USB flash memory drives.

The malware disabled important security features, such as antivirus software and automated update systems, and blocked users from downloading fixes. At the same time it exploited a weakness in Microsoft's server software to infect computers on the same network.

Conficker became the fastest-spreading malware known then, eventually found in almost every country. Outbreaks were reported from the armed forces of the UK, France and Germany, the British House of Commons and UK police forces. In the US, the Department of Homeland Security set up a Conficker Working Group of security experts to create strategies against similar outbreaks.

pages.title: Conficker: a sign of things to come

blocks.text: Conficker's authors were clearly not amateurs. They released new variants regularly to overcome weaknesses in the original malware, and took steps (including using **digital signatures**) to ensure that no one else could hijack their program.

Although Conficker caused a great deal of nuisance, it did not appear to do any actual harm to data - but it could have delivered other malware that would have attacked users. In many ways it was a harbinger of advanced criminal malware, such as **Cryptolocker**, that is a major threat to today's users.
A detailed analysis of Conficker's development and how its source was identified was published by Mark Bowden in the *New York Times* in June 2019.

blocks.q: Which of these did Conficker do? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Disabled antivirus software and automated updates
Blocked users from downloading fixes
Encrypted users' files and demanded a ransom
Used digital signatures so others could not hijack it
blocks.explain: Conficker disabled security features, blocked fixes and was protected by digital signatures. It did not appear to harm data - ransom-style attacks are associated with later malware such as Cryptolocker.

blocks.alt: A fisherman figurine on a keyboard with the word 'Password' on his fishing line
blocks.caption: Figure 7

blocks.text: Phishing is any attempt by attackers to steal valuable information by pretending to be a trustworthy party - a form of social engineering attack.
blocks.title: Phishing

blocks.text: An attacker might impersonate a bank to obtain credit card numbers or bank account details. The name comes from 'fishing' - as in fishing for information, luring people to disclose confidential information.

Phishing relies on people trusting official-looking messages, or conversations with apparently authoritative individuals. It is widespread and can be enormously costly: bank accounts emptied, credit references destroyed, personal or sensitive information lost.

Electronic phishing was described in the late 1980s, but the term became commonplace in the mid 1990s, when a program called **AOHell** allowed AOL users to impersonate other people (including the founder of AOL itself).

As more people connected, they received messages that looked very much like those from genuine banks, stores and government departments. Many did not realise that email addresses can be faked and electronic data easily copied - an email with your bank's logo is not necessarily from your bank.

Phishing emails may be indiscriminate. The phisher claims there is a problem with an account, adds plausible details such as the bank's logo and address, and sends it to millions of people. A few recipients will bank there, click the link or phone the number, and begin giving away further personal information.

pages.title: What to do if an email worries you

blocks.text: If you receive a worrying email from an organisation such as a bank or shop that you use, **do not click on or follow the links in the message**. Instead:

items: get in touch with their customer services department, or
log in to your account through their website - type in their web address or use your list of favourite sites, or
use their published phone number.

blocks.text: Most organisations have a published policy of not asking for sensitive information such as your password by email or phone, so be suspicious of anything that contravenes this policy.

blocks.q: An email that appears to be from your bank asks you to confirm your details via a link. What is the safest response?
options: Click the link but check the page looks genuine before typing anything
Reply to the email asking if it is real
Ignore the link and contact the bank via its own website address or published phone number
Forward it to friends to see if they got it too
blocks.explain: Never follow links in a suspicious message; contact the organisation through a route you already trust.

blocks.text: Email still accounts for most phishing, but the technique is also used on **social media sites** and in **text messages**. The same rules apply: if in doubt, go to the official site and contact the company through its published links.

A spear phishing attack is phishing targeted at individuals or specific parts of an organisation. It depends on detailed information about the target - for example, using recent emails to craft a plausible reply that appears to come from the target's colleagues.
blocks.title: Spear phishing

blocks.text: Attackers may also post links to malware-infected software in personal messages on social media. This is especially common after major disasters or during fast-breaking news, when people click interesting-looking links without thinking.

blocks.alt: Cartoon of a fishing boat whose net has caught letters and papers
blocks.caption: Figure 8

blocks.text: Phishing is just one type of **spam** email, which clutters mailboxes and often delivers unsuitable or even illegal content. Spam is another consequence of the early internet being developed by people who trusted one another.

Most email is moved around the world using the **Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)**, a standard template of commands and formatting that lets different mail programs understand one another. Protocols specify a set of special messages that computers exchange to achieve a particular function - here, delivering email.

SMTP was defined when the internet had very few users, so it included no way for computers to **authenticate** one another. A later extension, **SMTP-AUTH**, addressed this - but it was not required, so almost all mail servers still accept unauthenticated messages.
Spoofing is changing the information stored in email 'envelopes' so a spammer can disguise their actual address - for example, replacing their own sender address with that of TrustedBank.
blocks.title: Spoofing

blocks.text: Since SMTP servers perform no authentication, they simply pass on the email without checking that it really came from TrustedBank. Newer technologies let genuine senders authenticate messages so the recipient's mail server can check them, but only about half of all mailboxes have any protection against spoofing.

With a fast network (or, increasingly, a botnet) spam costs the sender almost nothing. Only a tiny fraction of people respond, but the volume makes it pay. An estimated seven trillion spam messages - over 85% of all email - were sent in 2011; by 2018 spam was estimated at 55% of messages. ISPs and companies must buy far more bandwidth and storage than legitimate use needs.

blocks.q: Because SMTP-AUTH exists, almost all mail servers now refuse unauthenticated email.
blocks.explain: SMTP-AUTH was never required, so almost all mail servers still accept unauthenticated messages - which is what makes spoofing possible.

blocks.alt: Example phishing email from 'TrustedBank' addressed to 'Dear valued customer', asking the reader to verify personal information via a link
blocks.caption: Figure 9 - an example of what could be a phishing email

blocks.text: A phishing attack may look plausible at first glance, but some tell-tale signs should make you very cautious:

items: **Spelling mistakes** - many phishing emails are sent from countries where English is not the main language, and give themselves away with imprecise English and spelling errors. But many use excellent English.

**Who is it to?** Many use 'Dear valued customer' or 'Dear user' because they cannot personalise. Your bank should use your name - although data breaches mean a phisher may know your personal details too.

**Poor quality images** - fuzzy images, or your information shown as an image rather than text, suggest copying from screens. But high-quality images are easy to obtain, so a good image proves nothing.

**Content of the email** - in almost all countries banks will not email you about problems with your account, because email is fundamentally insecure. Watch for a false sense of urgency claiming your account is at risk if you don't act quickly.

**Links** - the text of a link is not the same as its destination. Hover over the link (don't click) and the real address appears at the bottom of the window or in a small pop-up. Some fake links even show a genuine address on hover but use code in the page to send your click elsewhere.

blocks.alt: Email from 'ePay' reporting an unauthorised transaction; the link reads www.epay.com/confirm but hovering shows www.epay-secure-check.com/en/login.php
blocks.caption: Figure 10 - a phishing email claiming to come from the fictional ePay site

blocks.text: This message claims to come from a fictional site, ePay, about unauthorised activity on your account. The link says it goes to ePay's site, but the real address is slightly different and unlikely to be owned by ePay.

blocks.q: Hovering over the 'www.epay.com/confirm' link shows 'www.epay-secure-check.com/en/login.php'. What does this tell you?
options: Nothing - big companies often use several web addresses
The link destination differs from its text, a strong sign of phishing
The email must be genuine because it shows a secure address
Only that the link is broken
blocks.explain: The text of a link and its destination can differ. An unfamiliar destination address is a classic sign of a phishing email.

pages.title: Be suspicious - and check your address

blocks.text: The rules: be suspicious, and look at the details of the message - the language, the quality of the images and where the links actually take you. Banks and shops will always prefer you to call and check rather than risk your security.

Check your email address on **haveibeenpwned.com**. Addresses on a breached list are much more likely to receive spam. If yours is listed, assess what related data may have been revealed. You may need to change passwords that use that address - especially if you reused passwords - or even stop using it.

blocks.title: Check your email address
blocks.prompt: Check your email address on haveibeenpwned.com. Was it found in any breaches? What data was revealed, and what will you do about it?
blocks.model: If your address appears in a breach, find out what data (passwords, names, phone numbers) was exposed. Change the password for that service and for any other account where you reused it, and consider two-factor authentication. Expect more spam and phishing at that address, and in serious cases consider stopping using it.
points: Check whether the address appears in a breach
Identify what related data was revealed
Change passwords that use that address, especially reused ones
Expect more spam/phishing and consider retiring the address

pages.title: 2.5 Emails are not the only phish

blocks.alt: A keyboard whose keys show emojis instead of letters
blocks.caption: Figure 11

blocks.text: Malware is not spread solely through email - it will be spread through any means possible:

items: with **pirated material** such as illegal copies of software, video games and movies
by clicking links on websites - especially sites distributing illegal software, videos and pornography

through annoying **pop-up windows** claiming to have found problems with your computer (they probably haven't - but it's a great prompt to run your antivirus software and remind yourself what a genuine alert looks like)

blocks.text: A recent trend is malware spread through social networking services - like Cory's experience of the direct message on Twitter in Week 1. Once on a machine running social networking software, the malware **masquerades as the real user** and posts messages containing links to sites that distribute more malware.

This relies on social engineering: people are highly likely to click links they think come from friends. Most of these infections exploit weaknesses in **client software** rather than the web versions of the networks, so keep social networking apps (such as the Facebook app for mobile devices) up to date.

blocks.q: Most social networking malware infections have exploited weaknesses in client software, such as mobile apps, rather than the web versions of the networks.
blocks.explain: That is why it is important to keep social networking client software up to date.

pages.title: 2.6 The role of malware in click fraud

blocks.alt: A pile of banknotes in different currencies
blocks.caption: Figure 12

blocks.text: Most modern malware has malicious intent: to damage a computer's operating system or data, to steal information from a user - or, increasingly, from **online advertisers**.
Online advertising is big business: more than £16 billion was spent in the UK in 2011, expected to exceed £26 billion in 2020. It is cheap compared with print and lets advertisers target individuals.

The most common advertising model is 'pay per click', where advertisers pay site owners only when a user clicks an advert. Click fraud subverts this by generating clicks that don't come from genuine customers, or by hijacking clicks meant for a genuine advertiser. It accounts for more than 20% of all clicks.
blocks.title: Click fraud

blocks.text: Botnets of computers around the world can generate false clicks, siphoning money through layers of publishers and redistributors to hide its destination. Two common modes:

items: Clicking on a targeted company's ads on genuine sites to waste its advertising budget - the perpetrator collects no income.

Setting up hundreds or thousands of websites (often copied content), signing up for advertising such as Google AdSense, then paying a bot network to click the ads and collecting a share of the revenue.

blocks.text: One click raises very little, but millions add up. In 2011 the FBI broke an Estonia-based operation that had infected more than four million computers in 100 countries and stolen over $14 million. In 2016 a Russian group created 6,000 websites whose bots 'watched' over 300 million video ads a day, defrauding advertisers of close to four million dollars a day.

blocks.q: In the second mode of click fraud, how does the criminal make money?
options: By selling stolen advertising budgets
By having bots click ads on their own websites and collecting a share of the ad revenue
By charging victims to remove adware
By clicking competitors' ads on genuine sites
blocks.explain: The criminal builds many sites, signs up for advertising and uses a botnet to click the ads, collecting the publisher's share.

blocks.alt: Cartoon of angry computer characters with a frightened user
blocks.caption: From the botnet animation

blocks.title: Botnets: an animation
blocks.note: A talking computer warns that clicking an unsafe link lets an attacker drop a Trojan, a drive-by download or other malware and turn your computer into a 'zombie' - controlled without your knowledge to steal your identity or send spyware and spam. Many zombies form a botnet or 'zombie army'. Warning signs: the computer runs slower than normal, behaves erratically, or shows unexpected internet activity; check Task Manager, or disconnect from the network and see if it behaves differently. Prevention: don't click unsafe links or open attachments you're unsure of; keep antivirus and anti-spyware software up to date, from a reputable source (rogue antivirus can be malware in disguise); run a full scan; turn your firewall on; and if all else fails, ask an expert.

blocks.text: A botnet is a group of computers that coordinate their activity over the internet. Botnets are created using malware that gives an attacker control over the computers.
blocks.title: Botnet

blocks.text: Botnets are commonly used to gather information from the computers (e.g. usernames and passwords) and to launch attacks on others - sending spam, or flooding a website with so many requests that the server cannot cope, known as a **denial-of-service attack**.

A single piece of malware can do enormous damage, but when thousands or millions of computers run the same program the effects can be devastating. There are harmless botnets (for example for Internet Relay Chat, IRC), but the vast majority are created by malware.

Botnets spread through viruses and worms. Once installed, the malware contacts a **control computer**. The infected computer - a **zombie** - then does nothing except periodically check for instructions, so it raises no suspicion while the botnet grows to tens of thousands of zombies.
Later the control computer orders the botnet to wake up. Often the creators have sold or rented the botnet to another group.

Botnets have flooded the internet with spam, committed fraud against advertisers and carried out **distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)** attacks on companies and governments. Being so large and widely distributed, they are very hard to tackle.

blocks.q: Why do zombie computers in a growing botnet usually go unnoticed?
options: They only infect computers that are switched off
They do nothing except periodically check for instructions from the control computer
Antivirus software cannot scan them
They delete themselves after each attack
blocks.explain: Until the control computer wakes them, zombies appear to be doing nothing, so they don't raise suspicion.

blocks.alt: Illustration of two laptops facing each other with robots firing lasers
blocks.caption: Figure 13

blocks.title: Confessional: have you been infected?
blocks.prompt: It's time to confess! Has your computer ever been infected with malware? Do you know the name of the malware? Was it a virus, worm or Trojan? What happened, and what were the consequences?
blocks.model: Answers are personal. A useful reflection names the malware if known, classifies it (virus - attached to a program; worm - standalone and spread over the network; Trojan - disguised as legitimate software), explains how it probably got in (attachment, link, pirated software, pop-up) and what it did. Finish by noting what you'd do differently now.
points: Describes what happened and its consequences
Classifies the malware as virus, worm or Trojan
Identifies how it probably got in
Notes what you would do differently
blocks.hint: If you discuss this with others, don't share personal information, including the name of the company you work for.

blocks.alt: A syringe needle inserted into a vaccine bottle
blocks.caption: Figure 14

blocks.text: The growth in malware has been matched by explosive growth in software to stop it. So-called **antivirus software** (which actually targets a range of malware) is a multi-billion pound business, with many commercial and free packages.

Operating system developers are also building in security features that try to stop malware running at all. And you can do a lot yourself: install antivirus software, keep software up to date, watch for the signs of phishing and adopt new security developments.
Before installing or changing anti-malware software, check reviews - of free and paid packages - from reputable, independent organisations: av-test.org, selabs.uk and av-comparatives.org.

blocks.alt: Toy soldiers surrounding and guarding a laptop
blocks.caption: Figure 15

blocks.text: Antivirus software aims to detect, isolate and if necessary delete malware before it can harm data. The two most common techniques are **signatures** and **heuristics**.
A malware's signature is a distinctive pattern of data either in memory or in a file.
blocks.title: Signature

blocks.text: Antivirus can only detect malware whose signature has been identified and published. Between release 'into the wild' and the signature update, malware can exploit so-called **'zero day'** vulnerabilities. Authors often release variants with different signatures, and sophisticated malware can change its own program (it is **polymorphic** or **metamorphic**) without affecting how it works.

Heuristics use rules to identify viruses based on previous experience of the behaviour of known viruses. Heuristic detection may run suspicious programs in a **virtual machine** (a software recreation of a physical computer) and look for typical malware operations, such as replicating itself or overwriting key operating system files - or it may revert the program to source code and look for malware-like instructions.
Unlike signatures, heuristics can detect **new** malware just from its behaviour. Their drawback is that they draw conclusions only from past experience, so radically new malware can pass unnoticed.

blocks.q: What is the main advantage of heuristic detection over signature detection?
options: It never produces false alarms
It can detect new malware for which no signature exists, from its behaviour
It does not need to run any code
It catches every radically new piece of malware
blocks.explain: Heuristics need no specific knowledge of individual malware - but radically new behaviour can still slip through.

blocks.text: Antivirus software is essential, but it is not a complete solution. It has occasionally contained bugs - being inaccurate, failing to update or consuming huge amounts of computer power. These problems are rare, easily fixed and much less serious than the risk from malware.
Not all anti-malware software is equally good, and there is even **fake anti-malware** for sale, especially for mobile devices. Check reviews from av-test.org, selabs.uk or av-comparatives.org.

In October 2019 the BBC reported that British police, Indian police and Microsoft had shut down two Indian call centres using web pages and phone calls to sell fake computer security services. Victims lost thousands of pounds; the City of London Police say over 2,000 such cases are reported to Action Fraud every month.
The police offered these tips (BBC, 2019):

items: Always check out callers, especially cold callers claiming to be Microsoft, your telephony provider or internet service provider.
Legitimate organisations will encourage you to call back via a number you've obtained from a trustworthy source.
Don't assume the number displayed on your phone is accurate - it can be spoofed to look like a UK or trusted caller.
Don't call phone numbers on pop-up messages saying there is a problem with your computer.

blocks.q: If your phone shows a UK number for a caller claiming to be from Microsoft, you can trust that the call is genuine.
blocks.explain: Caller numbers can be spoofed. Call back on a number you obtained from a trustworthy source.

blocks.alt: Six computer screens showing padlocks and words such as privacy, password and protection
blocks.caption: Figure 16

blocks.text: If you don't have antivirus software, installing some should be a high priority. Windows 10 has **Windows Defender** built in, which got a top rating from AV-Test in June 2019. There are good free packages too, but check one meets your needs:

items: **Is it compatible with your computer?** - right for your operating system and computer.
**Does it come from a reputable source?** - e.g. a major security company such as Norton, Kaspersky, Sophos or AVG, or provided/recommended by your bank or ISP.
**Does it provide updates** to protect you against the latest malware?
**Have you checked the reviews?** - av-test.org, selabs.uk, av-comparatives.org.

blocks.title: Choosing antivirus software
blocks.prompt: Use the four criteria (compatibility, reputable source, updates, independent reviews) to research antivirus products and choose the best one for you. If you already have antivirus software, answer the questions for the program you have.
blocks.model: A good answer names a product and checks each criterion: it runs on your operating system and device; it comes from a recognised security company or is recommended by your bank or ISP (or is built in, like Windows Defender); it updates itself automatically against new malware; and it scores well in independent tests such as AV-Test, SE Labs or AV-Comparatives.
points: Compatible with your operating system and device
From a reputable source
Updates itself against the latest malware
Checked against independent reviews

pages.title: 3.3 Keeping your software up to date

blocks.alt: A smartphone lock screen showing a 'Software update' reminder
blocks.caption: Figure 17

blocks.text: Operating systems and applications are so large that they inevitably contain bugs, some of which could compromise your security.

Most companies issue regular updates to fix known problems. Major operating systems and some applications (such as Microsoft Office and the Adobe suite) automatically check for updates, prompt you to install them and perform the update. This process is sometimes called 'patching'.
blocks.title: Patching
Activity 1 Keeping your software up to date
blocks.prompt: How do you go about keeping one of the software applications on your computer or device up to date? Research the application online to find out if there is any additional information about keeping it up to date. (Allow about 15 minutes.)
blocks.model: Answers depend on the application. Typically you would check its settings for automatic updates and switch them on, know where to check manually (e.g. an 'About' or 'Check for updates' menu, or the app store), install security updates promptly, and look at the developer's support pages for how long the version will be supported.
points: Names the application and how it is updated
Turns on or checks automatic updates
Installs security patches promptly
Checks the developer's own guidance or support status

blocks.alt: An old typewriter with a DVD drive and a computer mouse attached
blocks.caption: Figure 18

blocks.text: Software's lifespan begins when it is released and ends when it is no longer supported and updated. It doesn't become completely unsafe at that point - you can often keep using it - but security risks may not be addressed. Employers may require you to move to an updated version.
The first effects you'll notice: telephone and internet support stops, bug reporting may be withdrawn, and cheap upgrades to later paid versions may no longer be available.

Most large software companies continue critical support for obsolete products for a time, but don't prioritise them: they fix and patch current software first, then test older products. Users of older products may be exposed to vulnerabilities for longer - and malware developers who know about unpatched bugs prefer to attack these weaker programs.

Windows 8.1 loses extended support on 10 January 2023. Windows XP has been unsupported since April 2014 despite wide use; XP and Vista have much higher infection rates than newer, more secure systems.

If you use end-of-life software, up-to-date **firewalls and antivirus** are essential, as is keeping key applications such as web browsers and email programs current. Even so, plan a move to more modern software: upgrades are relatively cheap (or free), and any cost should be weighed against what you could lose.

Even supported software is vulnerable if not updated. In 2017 the **WannaCry** ransomware infected thousands of computers globally; most were running Windows 7, which was still supported. An update fixing the vulnerability had been released months earlier, but many systems had not installed it.

blocks.q: What does the WannaCry case show?
options: Only end-of-life software can be attacked
Supported software is still vulnerable if updates are not installed
Antivirus software is unnecessary on supported systems
Windows 7 was never supported by Microsoft
blocks.explain: A fix had been released months before, but many still-supported Windows 7 systems had not been updated.

blocks.alt: An elaborate sandcastle
blocks.caption: Figure 19

blocks.text: Besides updates and antivirus, developers are building technologies such as **sandboxes** and **code signing** into everyday software to help mitigate malware.

A software sandbox is a way for computers to run programs in a controlled environment, with a constrained amount of memory and very limited access to resources such as operating system files, disks and the network.
blocks.title: Sandbox

blocks.text: In theory, software cannot break out of the sandbox, so even if malware tries to overwrite parts of the disk, the sandbox prevents it. Sandboxing is widely used in modern web browsers (Internet Explorer 10 onwards, Chrome) to stop internet content damaging files, and similar sandboxes exist for most browser plugins and Adobe Acrobat PDF viewer.
Code signing is a use of cryptography where software companies issue digitally signed copies of their programs that recipients can check for authenticity.
blocks.title: Code signing

blocks.text: The designers of all three major operating systems (Microsoft Windows, Mac OS and Linux) use code signing to guarantee that updates are genuine, even if distributed on flash memory cards rather than directly from the publisher. You'll learn more about digital signatures later in the course.

Windows uses code signing for components such as hardware drivers, which have direct access to the heart of the operating system. Apple goes further: Mac OS 10.8 onwards can restrict users to running only programs certified by the Apple App Store - more secure against malware, but it may restrict choice and block some unsigned third-party apps.

blocks.title: Match each protection term to its description

pairs.def: A distinctive pattern of data in memory or in a file that identifies known malware
Rules that identify malware from the typical behaviour of known malware
A vulnerability exploited before fixes and antivirus updates are available
Malware that changes its own program to disguise itself
Installing updates that fix known problems in software
A controlled environment with limited access to files, disks and the network
Digitally signing programs so recipients can check they are authentic

blocks.q: Which type of malware is a standalone application that copies itself across network connections?
options: Virus
Worm
Trojan
Adware
blocks.explain: A worm is self-replicating like a virus, but unlike a virus it is a standalone application.

blocks.q: Phishing is best described as...
options: software that forces you to view adverts
an attempt to steal valuable information by pretending to be a trustworthy party
flooding a website with requests
a program that copies itself into applications
blocks.explain: Phishing is a social engineering attack in which attackers impersonate a trustworthy party.

blocks.q: A link that displays a genuine-looking address is always safe to click.
blocks.explain: Link text can differ from its destination, and some fake links even show a genuine address on hover while code sends your click elsewhere.

blocks.q: What is a distributed denial-of-service attack?
options: A botnet flooding a target with so many requests that its servers cannot cope
An email pretending to come from a bank
Malware that encrypts files
Changing the sender address in an email envelope
blocks.explain: Botnets are used to swamp websites of companies and governments with requests.

blocks.q: Which of these are recommended when choosing antivirus software? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Check it is compatible with your computer
Check it comes from a reputable source
Choose one that never updates so it stays stable
Check independent reviews
blocks.explain: Good antivirus updates itself regularly to protect you against the latest malware.

blocks.q: Why do attackers prefer to target end-of-life software?
options: It is always more popular
Known bugs may remain unpatched for longer
It has no network access
It cannot run antivirus software
blocks.explain: Older products are fixed last, if at all, so their users stay exposed to known vulnerabilities for longer.

blocks.alt: Silver spider-like robots on a red circuit-board pattern
blocks.caption: Figure 20

blocks.text: This week you took a closer look at malware - viruses, worms and Trojans - how it gets into computers through phishing, spam, pirated software and social networks, and why it is created, from curiosity to click fraud and botnets. You also saw ways of keeping attackers from infecting your devices: antivirus software, updates, sandboxes and code signing.

Next week you'll delve deeper into the technologies that underpin information security, starting with how to protect the networks we depend on for transmitting digital information and accessing online services.
Optional further reading: 'Keep a clean machine' (StaySafeOnline) - basic precautions to take before you go online.

chapters.title: Week 4: Networking and communications
chapters.summary: How data moves across the internet in datagrams, wireless networks and their security, TCP/IP, IP addresses and DNS, and why the internet is not the world wide web.

blocks.text: Over the past three weeks you've explored many potential threats to your digital life, and ways of keeping attackers from impersonating you or infecting your devices with malware. Now you'll delve deeper into the technology that underpins information security, starting with how to protect the internet itself.

blocks.title: Cory Doctorow introduces Week 4
blocks.note: Cory explains that this week focuses on the network security problems that can affect the internet. By the end of the week you'll be aware of some of the networking standards that allow different devices to connect to the internet and exchange information, be able to explain how data is transmitted across networks, and understand the difference between the internet and the world wide web.

blocks.alt: Cory Doctorow speaking in front of a wall of books and pictures
blocks.caption: Cory introduces networking and communications.

blocks.text: By the end of this week you will be able to:

items: explain how data is transmitted across networks, including wireless networks
describe some of the networking standards (protocols) that let devices connect and exchange information
describe some security problems that affect networks, and how encryption helps
explain the difference between the internet and the world wide web

blocks.alt: Photograph of Vinton Cerf
blocks.caption: Figure 1 - Vinton Cerf

blocks.text: The internet is not a single entity with a single owner. It comprises a **hierarchy of individual networks** connected to one another - from local area networks (LANs) in businesses and universities to the telephone and data networks linking cities and countries by fibre optic cables and satellite links.
A definition often used is that the internet is a network of networks.
blocks.title: The internet

pages.title: Vinton Cerf on the birth of the internet

blocks.title: Audio: Vinton Cerf, a pioneer of the internet
blocks.note: Vint Cerf (Google's chief internet evangelist, often called a 'father of the internet' - a title he resists, saying there are many fathers) recalls working as a UCLA graduate student to put the first computer on the ARPANET, a 1969 network linking US university research departments. He explains that 'protocol' is borrowed from diplomacy: computer protocols are simply conventions for communication between computers. Data was chopped into packets that could travel by different routes and be recombined. When packet radio and satellite networks followed, Bob Kahn and Cerf designed TCP/IP (sketched on the back of an envelope in 1973) so computers on different networks could communicate, via gateways - today's routers. In 1977 three networks first worked together; in January 1983 all ARPANET computers had to switch to the new protocols. His one regret: choosing a 32-bit address space (about four billion addresses) in 1977.

blocks.text: The easiest way to understand how the Internet works is to think of Internet packets as electronic postcards... they don't necessarily arrive in the same order they were sent... Some of them get lost.

Cerf explains TCP with an analogy: imagine sending a novel using only postcards. You cut the pages up, **number** the postcards so they can be put back in order, **keep copies** in case some get lost, ask for **acknowledgements**, and use **time-outs** - if you hear nothing, you resend. That is basically how TCP works, only electronically and much faster.
Two key factors shaped the design of the internet:

items: **No central controlling computer.** Each computer on the network is assumed to have the same authority as every other.

**Delivery despite failures.** Information should get between any two computers even if some machines have failed (or, given its Cold War origins, been blown to pieces). With many alternative routes, data need not take the most direct path - it can go round damaged parts of the network.

blocks.q: Which were key design factors of the internet? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A central controlling computer with authority over all others
Each computer has the same authority as every other
Information can still be delivered if some machines fail
Data must always take the most direct route
blocks.explain: The internet has no central controller, and its many alternative routes let data avoid damaged parts of the network.

pages.title: 1.1 How data moves around the internet

blocks.alt: Diagram of a hierarchy of routers connecting groups of computers
blocks.caption: From the video on routing

blocks.title: How data is routed across the internet
blocks.note: The internet is thousands of separate networks owned by governments, corporations and individuals, all understanding a small number of protocols - chiefly IP (to transmit information) and TCP (a structure for sending data). It is a hierarchy: individual users and LANs; then internet service providers or corporate networks; then telecommunication companies that own the cables; the top tier is the 'internet backbone'. TCP breaks data into datagrams carrying sender and recipient addresses and a serial number. A local router looks up the destination in its address table; if unknown, it forwards the datagram to a higher-level router, possibly up to the backbone, then down to more local routers. Routers constantly share their status and reroute around congestion or failures, so parts of one file can take completely different routes. At the destination, TCP uses the serial numbers to reorder the data and requests copies of missing or damaged datagrams. (Note: the video's first example packet is addressed to 6.7.8.104; the two later examples route a packet to a local host, 1.2.3.104, and a remote host, 6.7.8.101.)

blocks.text: The internet is resilient to failures of individual computers - the **nodes** of the network - and of the connections between them - the **links**.

Instead of using a dedicated circuit for all the information, internet traffic is split up and may take any number of routes through the network, moving from origin to destination by a series of **hops**.

Routers at higher levels only need to examine the first part of a destination address to know where to forward a datagram. Because routers keep rerouting around congestion, TCP and IP together offer an extremely reliable way of sending data over what might be an unreliable network.

blocks.q: All the datagrams that make up one file must travel by the same route across the internet.
blocks.explain: Routers constantly reroute traffic, so datagrams from the same file can take completely different routes and are reordered by TCP at the destination.

blocks.alt: A pile of colourful envelopes
blocks.caption: Figure 2

blocks.text: When data such as a picture, movie or document is sent over the internet, it is not sent as a single chunk. It is split into small, uniformly sized blocks called **datagrams**, sometimes called **packets**.

Imagine posting a large book to a friend using only small envelopes. You tear the book into pieces, put each in an addressed envelope and number the envelopes. They may travel via the same sorting offices and arrive on the same day, or take different routes and arrive on different days - but your friend can still recreate the book once all have arrived.
Different datagrams are used on the internet, but they share a similar structure. One envelope and its contents correspond to a single datagram:

items: the **header** (the envelope) holds the sender's and recipient's addresses, a unique number, a date stamp and some error correction information
the **payload** (the contents) holds the actual information being delivered

blocks.text: The address is an IP number. You can look up an address with a **'whois'** service, such as whois.domaintools.com. Searching for open.ac.uk returns the IP address 137.108.200.90, shows the domain belongs to The Open University, located in Milton Keynes, England, hosted on an Apache server.

blocks.q: Which part of a datagram contains the actual information being delivered?
options: The header
The payload
The date stamp
The error correction information
blocks.explain: The header is like the envelope (addresses, number, date stamp, error correction); the payload is the contents.

blocks.text: Each datagram passes through a series of computer nodes forming the backbone of the internet. There are many thousands of nodes and often many routes between them. Each node has an IP address; looking it up with 'whois' may give a geographical location, only a country, or nothing at all.

Most computer systems can run software that follows the route from your computer to a destination and lists the nodes it passes through - usually called **Traceroute** (see wikihow.com/Traceroute for how to run it).
Rather than looking up each node yourself, you can paste Traceroute's output into an online mapping utility (such as the traceroute mapper at peter-thomson.com) to plot the route on a map.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Datagrams
blocks.prompt: Spend about 10 minutes using Traceroute (and a traceroute mapper) to explore the routes to some Australian organisations: the University of Sydney (usyd.edu.au) and the Sydney Morning Herald newspaper (smh.com.au). Then use whois.domaintools.com to locate the Sydney Morning Herald. Where did the routes end? How many stages did your information take, and did anything surprise you?
blocks.model: The route to the Sydney Morning Herald website does not terminate in Australia. A '.au' address is an Australian domain - auDA requires licensees to have some connection with Australia - but where the site is hosted is a different question from who uses the URL (a '.eu' site could be hosted by Google in the USA). Heavily used sites may also be cached on computers closer to the user. Nodes increasingly hide their location for security, or report only a country (sometimes the wrong one, from factory defaults), and routes change over time. usyd.edu.au's whois shows: IP Location - New South Wales - Sydney - University Of Sydney.
points: The SMH route did not end in Australia
A country domain does not mean the site is hosted in that country
Sites may be cached or served from several locations
Nodes often hide or misreport their location, and routes change
blocks.hint: Allow about 15 minutes. Information is not necessarily coming from where you might expect it to.

blocks.alt: A tall mast with satellite dishes and antennas above a city
blocks.caption: Figure 4

blocks.text: Early networks depended on wires, but engineers soon realised it would be useful to use wireless (radio) connections to create local networks. Wireless local area networks are now commonplace and known as **Wi-Fi**, after the trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance that certifies compatible products.

Wi-fi is in laptops, tablets and smartphones and an ever wider range of goods: eBook readers, smart TVs, burglar and smoke alarms. It lets devices such as computers and printers form a **local area network (LAN)** with signals sent through the air as radio waves instead of through cables.

'Wi-fi' refers to wireless LAN technology compliant with the **802.11** family of standards maintained by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). Routers show variants such as 802.11b, 802.11g and 802.11n.
In wireless LANs, devices (nodes) are called **stations**, since each acts as a radio station with a transmitter and receiver.
To connect, a station needs the name of the network - its service set identifier (SSID). The 'service set' is the set of wireless devices served by a particular wireless LAN.
blocks.title: SSID

blocks.text: The SSID lets nodes distinguish their network from others in the same space - for example, phone companies offering free wi-fi in airports use it so customers join the right network. In your list of available SSIDs, some show padlocks; more on that shortly.

blocks.q: What is the purpose of an SSID?
options: To encrypt data sent over wi-fi
To name a wireless network so devices can tell it apart from others nearby
To give each device a unique IP address
To measure signal strength
blocks.explain: The SSID is the network's name; it lets nodes distinguish their wireless LAN from others operating in the same physical space.

pages.title: 2 Is your private information really private?

blocks.alt: Reporter Sarah Smith presenting outside a building
blocks.caption: From the Channel 4 News report

blocks.title: Channel 4 News: hacking phones over wi-fi
blocks.note: Reporter Sarah Smith invites students to a free lunch. Hidden next door, security experts Glenn Wilkinson and Daniel Cuthbert use a small receiver attached to a laptop to create bogus wi-fi networks that look like familiar trusted ones. The students' phones automatically join, sending all their traffic through the hackers' laptops. The experts see their Facebook pages, read an unencrypted Yahoo email inbox, and identify places the phones had previously connected to wi-fi (one student had been to the States, another to Romania) - effectively tracking them. The students are shocked; one says she will now turn off wi-fi when out. Cuthbert's advice: be more aware of what you're connecting to - smartphones leak a lot of information - and criminals are already abusing this technology with advanced malware to get into people's email and computers.

blocks.text: We all hope the information we send wirelessly is private, but is it? Channel 4 News learned personal information about unsuspecting people by intercepting their supposedly private, but in reality completely public, wireless signals.
The attack worked because the hackers set up their own wi-fi hotspot that either advertised the name of a common hotspot provider, or that users chose to join as a 'free' network.
Be careful about the public wi-fi networks you connect to, and the types of information you access using them.

blocks.alt: The back of a wireless router with a cable plugged into the INTERNET port
blocks.caption: Figure 5

blocks.text: Internet routers move datagrams to their destination and are programmed to overcome congestion or failures by re-routing via any alternative path. So it is impossible to say with certainty which route a datagram will take outside a local network.

It will probably pass through several routers anywhere in the world, usually owned by a **third party**, not the sender or recipient. Datagrams can be copied as they pass through a router without alerting either party.

Packet sniffing is copying datagrams as they pass through the network. It has legitimate uses, such as analysing network performance and law enforcement, but the software is readily available to anyone - and with wireless networking, the sniffer no longer needs a wired connection.
blocks.title: Packet sniffing

blocks.alt: Three large satellite dishes silhouetted against the sky
blocks.caption: Figure 6

blocks.text: Wireless networks transmit over a medium shared by everyone, so anyone with a compatible receiver can eavesdrop. The three security essentials are all at risk:

items: **Confidentiality** - stopping an eavesdropper converting the signals back into the original message.
**Integrity** - a malicious user could sit between sender and receiver and modify or destroy messages: a **man-in-the-middle attack**.
**Availability** - an attacker could transmit lots of random data on the network's frequency, congesting it so others can't send data: a **denial-of-service (DoS) attack**.

blocks.text: A commonly used security mechanism is **encryption**: transforming information into a different form so that only the intended recipients can reverse the transformation and recover it - like a key that unlocks a door. Encryption can help ensure:

items: **Confidentiality** - a message encrypted with a particular key can only be decrypted with the same key, keeping it confidential between sender and receiver.
**Integrity** - it can prevent messages being modified without the receiver's knowledge.
**Authentication** - it can help prove the identities of the sender and receiver.

blocks.text: You'll look at encryption and decryption in more detail next week, when you learn how cryptography works.

blocks.q: An attacker floods a wireless network's frequency with random data so nobody else can send. Which security property is attacked?
options: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authentication
blocks.explain: This is a denial-of-service attack, which targets the availability of the network.

blocks.text: Most wi-fi security methods are based on encryption using a key known only to the nodes in the wireless network.

items: **WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy)** - the first mechanism, aiming for confidentiality comparable to a wired network. Since 2001 serious flaws have been found that let the key be computed within minutes using readily available software. Switch to more modern encryption wherever possible.
**WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2)** - used by most equipment in 2018, with a more secure key. It is the default configuration and must be supported by all devices compliant with 802.11.
**WPA3** - from 2019 new devices should start moving to this standard for higher security, though many public networks will keep running WPA2.

blocks.text: The only way to enhance your security on public wi-fi is a **Virtual Private Network (VPN)**, covered in Week 6.

blocks.title: Match each term to its description

pairs.def: Copying datagrams as they pass through the network
Intercepting and modifying messages between sender and receiver
Congesting a network so other users cannot send data
Early wi-fi encryption whose key can be computed within minutes
The default wi-fi encryption that all 802.11-compliant devices must support
Newer wi-fi standard adding higher levels of security from 2019
The only way to enhance your security on public wi-fi

blocks.alt: Three network cable plugs lying on a laptop keyboard
blocks.caption: Figure 7

blocks.title: Check your wireless networks
blocks.prompt: Use the network connection tool on your computer to see how many wireless networks are in range. How many use secure connections? Is your home network using WPA2 or WPA3? How do you connect when you're on the move (home wi-fi, mobile provider, coffee-shop wi-fi)? pages.title: 3 Why we need standards on the internet

blocks.alt: Aerial photograph of a complicated motorway junction
blocks.caption: Figure 8

blocks.text: Data sent over the internet crosses several hierarchies of networks, using different technologies from many providers and organisations. These networks must use a **standard form of communication** so information can pass from one to another.
How a network works internally is largely the business of its owner and users. But where it joins other networks and becomes part of the internet, it must conform to the internet's standards.
No single organisation owns the internet or dictates how it works - yet everyone with a network that forms part of it has to work to common standards, or data could not move between networks.

blocks.alt: The back of a computer with many cables plugged in
blocks.caption: Figure 9

blocks.text: The standards that allow different networks and communications equipment to talk to one another are formalised in digital rules known as communications protocols.
blocks.title: Communications protocols

blocks.text: For the internet the two most important are the **Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)** and the **Internet Protocol (IP)** - so inextricably linked they are often written together as **TCP/IP**.

TCP is responsible for ensuring data can be sent **reliably** over the internet. It uses software **ports** to keep data separate on the same computer - so you can browse a web page, collect email and stream music at the same time.

A 'port' can be a physical socket, like a USB port. For TCP, a port is a **number** indicating how data is handled when it reaches its destination. Many ports represent specific protocols. Common TCP ports:

items: **20 and 21** - File Transfer Protocol (FTP): sending and receiving files (20) and control (21)
**22** - Secure Shell (SSH): secure logins to computers
**25** - Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP): sending email
**80** - HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP): browsing web pages

blocks.text: Data from an application is divided into TCP datagrams, each containing the port number. TCP on the recipient's computer examines the port number to decide which application receives the data.

blocks.alt: Diagram: a request 'GET /pages/content/en/index.html' from a computer at 192.168.2.4 is split into three datagrams; each header holds destination IP/port 192.168.0.1 port 80 and source IP/port 192.168.2.4 port 3745, and the receiving computer reassembles the request
blocks.caption: Figure 10 - a web request split into datagrams, each carrying source and destination IP addresses and ports

blocks.title: Match each TCP port to its use

pairs.def: FTP control
FTP sending and receiving files
Secure Shell (SSH) for secure logins
SMTP for sending email
HTTP for browsing web pages

blocks.text: TCP's second major task is ensuring that all data sent is received. It waits for **acknowledgements** from the remote computer, and resends any datagram lost or damaged in transit. So TCP is **reliable - but relatively slow**.

Applications where timeliness matters more than absolute accuracy - streaming media, video games, video conferencing - use less reliable but faster protocols such as **UDP (User Datagram Protocol)**. You want an email to arrive with no gaps, but if you're streaming a TV programme it doesn't greatly matter if a few datagrams are lost.
TCP doesn't actually send and receive the information - that is done by a second protocol, most commonly IP.

blocks.q: Why would a video-conferencing app use UDP rather than TCP?
options: UDP is more reliable
Timeliness matters more than receiving every datagram, and UDP is faster
UDP encrypts all data
TCP cannot carry video
blocks.explain: TCP waits for acknowledgements and resends lost data, making it reliable but slower; UDP trades reliability for speed.

blocks.alt: A lorry driving along an empty road
blocks.caption: Figure 11

blocks.text: The **Internet Protocol (IP)** does the hard work of actually moving data across the internet. It is only concerned with moving data - it doesn't check that the data arrives; that is handled by TCP.
When IP receives data from TCP to send, it wraps the TCP datagram in its own IP datagram containing the sender's and receiver's addresses and some other information.

When IP receives data from the internet, it removes the IP datagram information and passes the contents to TCP, which checks and reorders them before passing them through the appropriate port to an application.

Addresses such as www.open.edu are for human convenience. Computers communicate using numeric **IP addresses** (or IP numbers). Every computer directly connected to the internet has a unique IP address. There are two major forms:

head: IPv4
IPv6
rows: Four numbers 0-255 separated by full stops, e.g. 192.168.0.1
A newer, much larger format, first outlined in 1998
Nearly exhausted by the number of connected devices
A theoretical 3.4 x 10^38 devices - any conceivable demand
Has long underpinned the internet; urgently needs replacing
Intended to replace IPv4; the transition is complex and far from complete

blocks.text: Some compatibility exists through **IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses**, where IPv4 addresses are stored in IPv6 format.
Not all IPv4 numbers are available. As well as large blocks reserved for specific users in the early days, some are used for **private** networks outside the internet:

Your computer allocates itself an address beginning **169.254...** if it can't connect to a local network. On a home internet connection it will almost certainly have an address beginning **192.168...**: your network hub has a genuine IP address, your devices have private addresses, and your modem alters the addresses on packets passing between your home network and the internet.

blocks.q: Your laptop shows the IP address 169.254.10.7. What does this most likely mean?
options: It is connected directly to the internet backbone
It could not connect to a local network and allocated itself an address
It is using IPv6
It is a public web server
blocks.explain: A computer allocates itself a 169.254... address when it is unable to connect to a local network.

blocks.alt: Close-up of '.uk' displayed on a screen
blocks.caption: Figure 12

blocks.text: When you type an address such as www.open.edu into a browser, it is translated into a unique IP address by a name server, called a Domain Name Server (DNS), located somewhere on the internet.
blocks.title: DNS

blocks.text: That IP address is then attached to every IP datagram destined for the Open University server.
Addresses are resolved from the **most general part to the most specific**, as the next example shows.

pages.title: Example: finding Bob at Big University

blocks.text: An email is being sent to Bob, who works in the coffee bar at Big University in America: **bob@coffee.big.edu**.

items: The sender's name server asks a computer that holds the addresses of American universities (most use **.edu**) for the IP number of **big.edu**.
The .edu name server replies with the IP number of the name server at Big University.
The sender's machine contacts the big.edu name server and asks for the IP number of the coffee shop computer used by Bob.
The big.edu name server replies with that address, so the IP datagrams can be correctly addressed and sent into the network.

blocks.q: DNS resolves an address starting with the most specific part (e.g. 'coffee') and working out to the most general (e.g. '.edu').
blocks.explain: The address is sorted from the most general part (.edu) to the most specific.

blocks.text: Until 2019, DNS requests were sent as **plain text** and could be intercepted even when the data being sent or requested was encrypted.

From 2019 DNS requests can be encrypted (**DNS over HTTPS**). In Firefox: Settings, then Network settings, and select the enable DNS over HTTPS checkbox. Chrome 78 was experimenting with the feature: browse to chrome://flags/, search for 'dns-over-https', enable it and restart the browser.

blocks.q: Why was DNS over HTTPS introduced?
options: To make websites load images faster
Because DNS requests were sent as plain text and could be intercepted
To replace IP addresses with names
To block all advertising
blocks.explain: Even when page data was encrypted, plain-text DNS requests revealed which sites were being looked up.

pages.title: 3.4 The internet is not the world wide web

blocks.alt: Tim Berners-Lee holding a glowing plasma ball
blocks.caption: Figure 13 - Tim Berners-Lee devised the specifications for URIs, HTTP and HTML

blocks.text: Saying 'I'm on the internet' while browsing is true but misleading. The internet dates from **1982** (with roots back to **1969**), but the world wide web only came into being in **1990**, thanks to Sir Tim Berners-Lee.

Before the web, fewer people used the internet (it took until 1998 for 100 million people to log on), commands had to be typed in, often cryptically, and what came back was plain text. The web made the internet usable without learning a new language, delivering rich text, graphics, animation and sound at the click of a button.

pages.title: The web is part of the internet

blocks.text: At its simplest, the world wide web is the part of the internet that can be accessed through the HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP).
blocks.title: World wide web

blocks.text: HTTP lets two computers exchange information as a series of **requests** (e.g. your computer asking for a course web page) and **responses** (the server delivering it). HTTP relies on TCP to set up the connection, and TCP uses IP to send and receive data. Web browsers are the most common applications that understand HTTP.

The web is an example of **hypertext** - documents joined by links. Each click uses HTTP to request a page from a web server via TCP **port 80**; the content comes back through port 80 and the browser formats it for you to read.

The web was designed from the start to be **open**, encouraging people to set up their own servers and write pages. All documentation for HTTP and related standards is publicly available, and the **HyperText Mark-up Language (HTML)** used to format web documents is fully documented online and easy to use.

Beyond the web, the internet carries many other services, including **email, instant messaging and file transfers**. Its flexibility comes from its underlying protocols: as long as information can be stored in IP datagrams - and just about anything can - it can be moved around the internet.

blocks.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the internet and the web?
options: They are two names for the same thing
The web is one service running over the internet, accessed through HTTP
The internet runs on top of the web
The web is older than the internet
blocks.explain: The internet (from 1982) carries many services; the web (from 1990) is the part accessed through HTTP.

blocks.title: Audio: Tim Berners-Lee on the world wide web
blocks.note: In 1980 Berners-Lee wrote ENQUIRE, a hypertext program. In 1989 at CERN, frustrated by incompatible documentation systems, he realised a global hypertext system could represent any of them without forcing a particular machine or format - give every document an identifier in one universal space. His boss let him write the program; with Robert Cailliau he spent two years refining the protocols. He explains a link: the identifier starts http:// (how to fetch it), then a computer name such as www.acme.com, which another computer translates into a number; your computer connects and sends a simple 'get' command, and the page comes back. The first public website launched in August 1991; the web did not suddenly explode - load on the first server, info.cern.ch, grew tenfold every year. Part two of his dream - machine-understandable information - still needed more technology: digital signatures, a web of trust and logical reasoning on the web.

blocks.text: Towards the end, Tim Berners-Lee mentions things the web needs to reach its full potential. One is **digital signatures**, which can be achieved using cryptography - the topic for next week.

chapters.summary: Plaintext, ciphertext and keys, symmetric and public key cryptography, encrypted email, common ciphers, hashing, digital signatures and certificates, and TLS/SSL for secure browsing.

blocks.title: Introduction to Week 5
blocks.note: Cory Doctorow reminds you that early in the course you looked at keeping digital information secret and untampered - confidentiality and integrity. This week focuses on cryptography, which secures information so it can be transmitted safely even over unsecured networks. You'll learn the basic terminology, how cryptography achieves different security goals (including securing your email and protecting your digital life), and how it is used in common applications such as the world wide web.

blocks.title: Cryptography
blocks.text: A specialised area of mathematics concerned with protecting information so that it can be transmitted and received securely even when there is a risk that a hostile third party might intercept or modify the data.
You have met cryptography earlier in the course as a technique that can help protect information. This week looks at this important aspect of cyber security in a little more detail.
By the end of this week you should be able to:

items: use the basic terminology of cryptography: plaintext, ciphertext, cipher, key, encryption and decryption
explain the difference between symmetric and public key (asymmetric) cryptography and the key distribution problem
describe how cryptography tools can be used to secure your email
explain how hashing, digital signatures and certificates help prove that data is genuine
explain the use of cryptography in common applications such as the world wide web (TLS/SSL)
identify where you could use cryptography to improve the protection of your digital life

blocks.text: Cryptography has a long history: from simple ciphers used by Julius Caesar to send military orders to his generals, to more sophisticated medieval ciphers that withstood most attacks until the late nineteenth century, to the famous Enigma codes of the Second World War.

blocks.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a number of women working at machines in an office
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Before computers, cryptography relied on people and machines

blocks.text: The development of computers in the twentieth century allowed far more complex means of encryption. Computers could perform:

items: the mathematical operations that underpin all cryptography
much more complex mathematics than could reasonably be expected of a human
much faster than a human
on much more data than a human could handle.

pages.title: Cryptography makes the modern world possible

blocks.text: Any data that can be represented in binary format (using 0s and 1s) can be encrypted by a computer. It is not an exaggeration to say that encryption makes much of the modern world possible. Commonplace applications include:

items: secure banking and payments systems - keeping your money safe when it is transferred between accounts, issued at ATMs or used to shop online
protecting conversations made over mobile telephones
safeguarding wireless networks that give access to the internet
securing files on hard disks and memory sticks
authenticating electronic documents
electronic voting
securing media files such as music or movies from piracy - known as Digital Rights Management (DRM)

blocks.q: Only text documents can be encrypted by a computer.
blocks.explain: Any data that can be represented in binary (0s and 1s) can be encrypted - music, movies, programs, files on disks and more.

blocks.alt: Close-up of an Enigma cipher machine showing its keyboard and lamp board
blocks.caption: Figure 2 An Enigma cipher machine

items: **Plaintext** - information that can be directly read by humans or a machine. A historic term from when encryption was used only for hardcopy text; nowadays it covers many formats including music, movies and computer programs.
**Ciphertext** - the encrypted data.

**Cipher** - the mathematics (or algorithm) responsible for turning plaintext into ciphertext and reverting ciphertext to plaintext. (You may see 'code' used - there is a technical difference, but it need not concern us now.)
**Encryption** - converting plaintext to ciphertext (occasionally called 'encipherment').
**Decryption** - reverting ciphertext to plaintext (occasionally 'decipherment').

The encrypted data
