A piece of information that determines the output of an encryption or decryption process

blocks.title: Keys
blocks.text: Pieces of information that determine the output from an encryption (or decryption) process.
A single cipher can produce an almost limitless number of different outputs with different key values. This allows secure communication even if the cipher itself is known to hostile third parties.

In fact, almost all ciphers are published in the scientific press or in standards documents. Making them available for widespread scrutiny lets many people check that they are secure and contain no weaknesses that could be exploited to compromise data encrypted with them.

blocks.alt: Abstract image of coloured numbers and patterns
blocks.caption: Figure 3 A key is just a string of bits

blocks.text: A computer encryption key is nothing more than a string of bits, each with a value of 0 or 1. A one-bit key has only two possible values: 0 and 1. A two-bit key has four: 00, 01, 10 and 11. Every extra bit **doubles** the number of possible keys, so a three-bit key has eight values (000 to 111).
The total number of keys is 2 to the power of the key length. An eight-bit key has 2^8 = 256 possible values.

blocks.q: How many possible values does a 10-bit key have?
blocks.explain: 2 to the power 10 = 1,024. Each extra bit doubles the number of keys.

blocks.text: Short keys are vulnerable to a **brute force attack** - just as you learned in Week 2 about passwords. A computer, or a number of computers, tries every possible key value until one produces recognisable plaintext.
Since computers can work through key values extremely rapidly, keys must be long enough to offer a very large number of possible values.
Where do keys live?

items: known to the user in the form of passwords
stored in a computer's hardware - such as the decryption keys in a DVD player that let it play encrypted movie disks
generated by a computer as and when needed - such as during a secure transaction on a shopping site

blocks.q: Keeping a cipher secret is the main thing that makes modern encryption secure.
blocks.explain: Almost all ciphers are published for scrutiny. Security comes from the key - which must be long enough to resist brute force - not from hiding the cipher.

pages.title: 1.3 The key distribution problem: Alice, Bob and Eve

blocks.title: The key distribution problem
blocks.note: Alice and Bob want a confidential relationship; Eve is an eavesdropper. Messages across the internet pass through many computers belonging to ISPs, employers or telecom companies - some in other countries, some untrustworthy. Eve can compromise one of them with a packet sniffer that copies every message to her without Alice or Bob knowing. Symmetric encryption (a single key to encrypt and decrypt - used today in DES, triple DES and AES for banking) protects them, but they must share the key: meeting in person isn't always possible, the post can be lost or intercepted, and armed couriers are so expensive that historically only governments and the largest companies could afford them. If Alice sends the key over the internet, Eve can copy it and read every message. Until the early 1970s this was thought to have no solution; the answer is asymmetric encryption, with a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt.

blocks.title: Symmetric encryption
blocks.text: Uses a single key both to encrypt plaintext to ciphertext and to decrypt ciphertext back to plaintext.

Traditionally, symmetric encryption suffered one enormous shortcoming: the sender or recipient had to create a key and send it to the other party. While in transit it could be stolen or copied by a third party, who could then decrypt anything encrypted with it.
Also, many key pairs are needed between communicating parties: **n(n-1)/2**, where n is the number of parties. Ten parties need 10(10-1)/2 = 45 key pairs; 100 parties would need 4,950.

This **key distribution problem** affected anyone wishing to use encryption until the 1970s, when a way of distributing keys without sending the keys themselves was developed independently by GCHQ in the UK and by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in the US. The British discovery was kept secret for years, so it is known as the **Diffie-Hellman key exchange**.
Symmetric methods remain very useful: encryption and decryption are extremely fast, ideal for large amounts of data.

blocks.q: Using n(n-1)/2, how many key pairs do 20 parties need to all communicate securely with each other?
blocks.explain: 20 x 19 / 2 = 190. The number of keys grows rapidly as more parties join.

pages.title: 1.4 Public key cryptography: the padlock analogy

blocks.title: Asymmetric cryptography
blocks.note: A thought experiment: Bob orders many identical padlocks and a single key that opens them all. He posts a padlock to anyone who asks but never gives away the key. Alice puts her document in a box and snaps Bob's padlock shut - now even she can't open it, so it is safe in the post. Only Bob's key opens it. The padlocks are the public key; Bob's key is the private key. Together they form a key pair, held on a computer's key chain. Key pairs are generated from information such as name and email plus random input (typing, network traffic, waggling the mouse). Alice and Bob exchange public keys; Alice encrypts with Bob's public key and only Bob's private key can decrypt. If Eve intercepts the ciphertext and tries Bob's public key, she gets rubbish - she would need to steal Bob's private key or brute force it, which could take billions of years.

blocks.title: Key pair
blocks.text: The **private key**, which the owner keeps safe and never distributes, and the **public key**, which can be sent to anyone they want to exchange encrypted information with.

Asymmetric (public key) cryptography side-steps the key distribution problem because each user creates their own keys. Unlike symmetric encryption, the two keys behave differently: only the public key can decrypt what the matching private key encrypted, and only the private key can decrypt what the matching public key encrypted. Crucially, one key cannot easily be worked out from the other.
Public keys can be sent as email attachments or uploaded to **public key chain servers**, which distribute large numbers of public keys freely.
To send a message, the sender gets the recipient's public key, encrypts the message with it and sends the ciphertext. The recipient uses their private key to restore the plaintext.

blocks.q: Alice wants to send Bob a secret document using public key cryptography. Which key does she encrypt it with?
options: Alice's private key
Alice's public key
Bob's public key
Bob's private key
blocks.explain: She uses Bob's public key, so that only Bob's private key - which never leaves Bob - can decrypt it.

blocks.text: Public key cryptography is popular because no initial secure exchange of secret keys is needed - users only ever exchange public keys. However, it is generally far slower than symmetric encryption, and because of a quirk in the underlying mathematics traditional public key techniques need far longer keys for the same level of protection.

head: Symmetric
Public key
rows: Key must reach the other party safely
Extremely fast; good for large data

blocks.text: A newer type, **elliptic curve cryptography**, can be just as secure as symmetric encryption using similar key lengths.

blocks.caption: Figure 4 'https' at the start of a web address

blocks.text: One part of everyday life that is not routinely protected by cryptography is the internet itself. Most emails and web pages are sent in plain view and can be intercepted and read by a malicious third party.

Encrypting the whole internet is unlikely: encryption and decryption take computer power, so there would be significant costs, and many applications - reading news, browsing shops - involve no sensitive information. Instead, applications selectively use cryptography for key tasks (such as payments), and users may choose it for extra purposes (such as securing email). Many websites encrypt data in transit, sometimes shown by a padlock in the address bar.

blocks.text: So far you have studied basic techniques that protect the confidentiality and integrity of information. How are they used in practice, for example for email?

items: **Transport-level encryption** encrypts the message between your device and the server that receives it. One of the most common is STARTTLS. However, messages may not be encrypted while sitting on a mail server.
**End-to-end encryption** keeps the message fully encrypted all the way from sender to recipient.

blocks.text: Internet banking and shopping sites routinely use encryption, but the tools to protect email are harder to install and configure. Most end-to-end tools depend on a collection of techniques called **Pretty Good Privacy (PGP)**, which includes symmetric and asymmetric algorithms. The **OpenPGP** standard, agreed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), helps vendors build systems that exchange encrypted information.

blocks.q: With transport-level encryption such as STARTTLS, your email is guaranteed to stay encrypted while stored on the mail server.
blocks.explain: Transport-level encryption protects the message between your device and the server; it may not be encrypted while sitting on a mail server. End-to-end encryption keeps it encrypted all the way.

A secure email service such as **ProtonMail** or **Tutanota** can hide the metadata linking sender and recipient.

blocks.text: Modern cryptography is growing steadily with its everyday use - surfing the internet, using a cash machine and so on. There are hundreds of schemes; some of the most notable follow.
DES (Data Encryption Standard)

Developed in the 1970s and adopted by the US National Bureau of Standards as the government standard for sensitive information. A symmetric cipher using **56-bit keys**. Because of its small key size, DES can now be brute forced in less than a day - the weakness that led to the adoption of other standards such as AES.
Triple DES

A variant giving extra security while staying compatible: three rounds of DES with three separate 56-bit keys. Widely used in e-commerce, online payments and Microsoft Outlook until 2018. Once expected to be secure until at least 2030, it is now considered insecure and was deprecated by NIST in 2017.

When DES was no longer adequate, the US government ran an open competition lasting five years. AES was adopted as a US government standard in 2001. It uses a combination of symmetric ciphers and **128, 192 or 256-bit keys**.
Some potential weaknesses have been identified, but most are theoretical: AES is easiest to break when it has not been implemented correctly, rather than by brute force.

Its specification is freely available, so AES is widely used commercially: protecting archive files, encrypting file systems (Windows 2000 onwards) and hard disks, and secure file transmission. Many microprocessors now include AES in their instruction sets to speed it up.

blocks.alt: A spiky, inflated blowfish (pufferfish)
blocks.caption: Figure 7 Blowfish

blocks.text: Developed in the early 1990s as a potential replacement for DES (AES became the agreed standard). Blowfish supports variable key lengths from **1 to 448 bits**. No successful attack on its full implementation is known, but weaknesses appear with relatively weak keys. The related twofish and threefish ciphers were designed to overcome these, although most users have switched to AES.

pairs.def: 1970s US standard using 56-bit keys; can now be brute forced in under a day
Three rounds with three separate 56-bit keys; deprecated by NIST in 2017
Chosen after a five-year open competition; 128, 192 or 256-bit keys
Early 1990s cipher with variable key lengths from 1 to 448 bits

pages.title: 3.1 Using cryptography to prove identity: hashing

blocks.text: Cryptography isn't just for hiding secrets: it can also authenticate data sent over an insecure network such as the internet. The process begins by checking that your copy of some data exactly matches the one you requested.

blocks.title: Hashing
blocks.text: The mathematical process of converting data of any size into data of fixed length known as the 'hash' (also called message digest, hash code, hash sum or hash value).

Hashing works in one direction only - you cannot deduce the original data from the hash. Its aim is not to preserve the data but to create a unique identifier for every piece of data. Authors may publish the hash of a file alongside it.

blocks.alt: List of long hexadecimal SHA-1 hash values beside GnuPG file names such as gnupg-2.0.22.tar.bz2
blocks.caption: Figure 9 SHA-1 hashes published by the GnuPG authors next to each file name

pages.title: Checking a hash, and broken algorithms

blocks.text: After downloading a file you can run your own copy of the hashing program (e.g. SHA-1). If your file exactly matches the original, the two hashes are identical. A change of a single bit gives a vastly different hash, revealing tampering - so the data should not be trusted.

The most widespread algorithms are **MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-2**. MD5 and SHA-1 are in common use but flawed: under specially controlled conditions 'collisions' occur, where two different pieces of data give the same hash. The MD5 weakness has been used in malware targeting Windows. Both can be considered 'broken'; the US government requires the newer **SHA-2**, which has shown no such weaknesses.

blocks.q: You download a program and your SHA-2 hash differs from the one the author published. What should you conclude?
options: The hash program is broken - use the file anyway
The file has been changed since it was hashed and should not be trusted
Hashes always differ slightly, so this is normal
The file is encrypted
blocks.explain: Even a one-bit change gives a vastly different hash, so a mismatch means the data has been altered (or corrupted) and should not be trusted.

blocks.title: Signatures and certificates
blocks.note: Encrypting with your private key doesn't hide secrets - anyone with the public key can decrypt it - but it proves the data could only have come from the holder of the private key, so it authenticates data. However, a public key is only tied to an email address: if Eve steals Bob's email address she can make keys in his name and send false documents or malware. Bob can prevent this by having a trusted third party (an individual, government or company) certify his key after he proves his identity with documents such as a passport. A certificate contains the public key, a unique serial number, the owner's name, the issuing agency's name and digital signature, issue and expiry dates, and a hash to check it hasn't been altered. Certificates authenticate software downloads such as app stores, and websites present them to browsers, which warn users if a certificate is invalid. Holders must renew before expiry - in November 2015 millions of Mac users could not update apps until Apple issued a new certificate.

blocks.text: Hashing shows data hasn't changed, but not who it came from. For that you need a **digital signature**: the sender's private key is used to encrypt the hash. Anyone with the matching public key can decrypt and compare it, and since it must have been produced by the private key holder, it provides authenticity.

pages.title: Case study 1: Alice signs her profit statement

blocks.text: Alice wants to send her company's quarterly profit statement to Bob, who works in the financial markets, for public announcement. Both want confidence that Eve has not intercepted and altered it.

blocks.alt: Diagram: Alice hashes the profit statement, encrypts the hash with her private key to make a digital signature and sends both to Bob. Bob decrypts the signature with Alice's public key, hashes the statement himself and compares the two hashes: equal means not modified, different means modified.
blocks.caption: Figure 10 How Alice signs the statement and Bob verifies it

blocks.text: Alice hashes the statement and encrypts the hash with her private key - the digital signature - and sends it with the statement (she may also encrypt both with Bob's public key to keep them secret). Bob decrypts with his private key if needed, decrypts the signature with Alice's public key to reveal the hash, hashes the statement himself and compares. If the hashes match, it wasn't altered en route.

blocks.q: In case study 1, which key does Bob use to decrypt Alice's digital signature?
options: Bob's private key
Bob's public key
Alice's private key
Alice's public key
blocks.explain: The signature was made with Alice's private key, so only her matching public key can decrypt it - which is what proves it came from her.

blocks.q: Which statements about a digital signature are correct?
options: It is a hash encrypted with the sender's private key
It keeps the message contents secret
It shows the message hasn't changed in transit
It proves the key really belongs to the named person
blocks.explain: A signature is an encrypted hash that reveals tampering and links data to a private key. It doesn't hide contents, and on its own it can't prove who owns the key - that needs a certificate (see case study 2).

blocks.text: Digital signatures don't give complete confidence about the author: someone could masquerade as the sender by producing their own key pair.

A digitally signed invoice arrives for Alice from 'Bob'. She uses Bob's public key from a public key server to check the signature; the hashes match, so she pays the account on the invoice. Weeks later, an angry Bob says he hasn't been paid - the money went to Eve.

What went wrong? Eve used Bob's personal information to create a new key pair in Bob's name and put the public key on a public key server. She signed the invoice with her matching private key. Alice trusted what she believed was Bob's signature.

blocks.q: If a signature checks out using a public key from a public key server, you can be sure the document came from the person named on the key.
blocks.explain: Anyone can create a key pair in someone else's name and upload the public key, as Eve did. A certificate from a Certificate Authority is needed to bind a key to its real owner.

pages.title: Digital certificates and the chain of trust

blocks.title: Digital certificate
blocks.text: A means of binding public keys to their owner, issued by a Certificate Authority (CA) that validates the owner's identity, binds the public key to the certificate and signs it with the CA's private key. The CA's public key is available to anyone who needs to check it.

Certificates still need a **chain of trust** to confirm they belong to who you think and haven't been compromised. Criminals have obtained certificates to sign software containing malware, and stolen certificates have been used too - Stuxnet was signed with certificates belonging to Realtek Semiconductor and JMicron Technology Corp.
Case study 3

With a CA, Eve can't simply create a key pair and claim it is Bob's. If she sends an invoice appearing to be signed by Bob, Alice's check with Bob's validated public key will fail, so she'd know something was wrong - and (hopefully) not pay Eve.

Scams increasingly involve fake invoices sent to businesses, or a senior manager being impersonated to persuade staff to pay the scammer. All businesses should ensure managers and directors have private and public keys, with public keys stored and displayed locally for everyone to use - and must use them to sign and validate all non-routine payment instructions. This is about the only way to avoid the scam reported by the BBC:

'Hey, the deal is done. Please wire $8m to this account to finalise the acquisition ASAP. Needs to be done before the end of the day. Thanks.' The employee thought nothing of it and sent the funds over... But alarm bells started to ring when the company that was being acquired called to ask why it had not received the money.

blocks.q: According to the course, what is about the only way for a business to avoid this kind of payment scam?
options: Only accept payment requests by email
Have managers sign non-routine payment instructions with keys whose public keys are held locally and checked
Use a faster bank transfer service
Encrypt the email subject line
blocks.explain: Signing and validating all non-routine payment instructions with known, locally stored public keys lets staff detect impersonation.

blocks.alt: Two hands shaking, surrounded by symbols such as @, an envelope, a speech bubble and a padlock
blocks.caption: Figure 11 A secure 'handshake'

blocks.text: Web traffic is not encrypted by default: pages pass as plaintext and can be intercepted. When online shopping began, companies had customers browse online and then phone in their credit card details.

The solution came in 1995 when Netscape announced the **Secure Socket Layer (SSL)** protocol, now replaced by **Transport Layer Security (TLS)**. Supported by all modern browsers, it allows confidential information to be exchanged over an insecure link.
TLS/SSL combines asymmetric and symmetric encryption:

items: **Handshake**: browser and server agree how to communicate, including the type of cryptography.
The server sends its public key and a digital certificate; the user's computer checks it is genuine and not expired.
The computer generates a **master secret**, encrypts it with the server's public key and sends it.
The server decrypts it with its private key. Both now use the secret to generate identical symmetric keys - the key itself never crosses the network.
Each sends a 'finished' message using the **session key**; the transaction (bank details, card numbers, addresses) then uses fast symmetric encryption.
At the end, both delete the session key. A new session uses a completely new key.

blocks.q: Why does TLS switch to a symmetric session key after the handshake?
options: Symmetric encryption is much faster for the actual data
Public key encryption can't encrypt credit card numbers
The certificate expires after the handshake
Symmetric keys are sent openly across the network
blocks.explain: Public key cryptography solves key exchange, but symmetric encryption is far faster for the transaction itself. The session key is never transmitted.

pages.title: What TLS/SSL does - and doesn't - tell you

blocks.text: TLS/SSL is now used by most websites. It is an automatic process between browser and server that keeps data safe in transit, giving users confidentiality and integrity without having to configure software or manage keys.

blocks.title: Not a seal of approval
blocks.text: TLS/SSL doesn't mean a site is genuine. Any website, including criminal ones, can now implement TLS/SSL for free.

blocks.q: A padlock and 'https' prove that a website is run by a legitimate organisation.
blocks.explain: They show the connection is encrypted. Criminal sites can use TLS/SSL for free too.

blocks.alt: A combination padlock and chain lying on a circuit board
blocks.caption: Figure 12 Locking down your connection

blocks.text: Browsers make it easy to see whether a site uses TLS/SSL by:

items: making secure addresses begin **https://** rather than http:// - the s stands for 'secure' (e.g. Gmail at https://mail.google.com; Google search at https://www.google.com, so your searches and results can't be seen by others)
showing a closed **padlock** symbol in or near the top of the browser window

Clicking the padlock shows connection and certificate details

items: **Firefox**: go to settings, then network settings, and select the 'enable DNS over HTTPS' checkbox.
**Chrome** (78 was experimenting with this, as mentioned in Week 4): browse to chrome://flags/, search for 'dns-over-https', enable it and restart the browser.

Asymmetric encryption using a key pair: a public key anyone may have and a private key the owner never shares
Trying every possible key value until recognisable plaintext is produced
A fixed-length value computed one-way from data of any size; any change to the data changes the hash
A hash encrypted with the sender's private key, proving origin and integrity

blocks.q: Which term describes the encrypted data?
options: Plaintext
Ciphertext
Cipher
Key
blocks.explain: Ciphertext is the encrypted data; the cipher is the algorithm that produces it.

blocks.q: Who independently solved the key distribution problem in the 1970s?
options: Netscape and Microsoft
GCHQ in the UK, and Diffie and Hellman in the US
NIST and the IETF
Julius Caesar's generals
blocks.explain: GCHQ's discovery was kept secret, so the method is known as Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

blocks.q: Why was DES replaced as a US government standard?
options: Its cipher was kept secret
Its 56-bit key is short enough to be brute forced
It could only encrypt text
It used public keys
blocks.explain: With modern computing power DES can be brute forced in less than a day, so AES was adopted.

blocks.q: Which hashing algorithm does the US government require because it has shown no collision weaknesses?
options: MD5
SHA-1
SHA-2
Blowfish
blocks.explain: MD5 and SHA-1 can produce collisions and are considered broken; SHA-2 is required.

blocks.q: What does a Certificate Authority do?
options: Encrypts all web traffic
Validates who owns a public key and signs a certificate binding the key to them
Stores everyone's private keys
Generates session keys for TLS
blocks.explain: The CA validates the owner's identity and signs the certificate with its own private key.

blocks.q: Why isn't the whole internet routinely encrypted?
options: Encryption is illegal for ordinary users
It would cost computing power and much traffic isn't sensitive
Ciphers are kept secret
Encryption only works on text
blocks.explain: Encrypting everything has significant computing costs and many uses, like reading news, don't involve sensitive information - so cryptography is used selectively.

blocks.text: This week focused on cryptography - a key security technique that lets you ensure the confidentiality and integrity of your data.

You have learned how cryptography tools can secure your email and can explain its use in common applications such as the world wide web. You should now be able to identify where you could use cryptography to improve the protection of your digital life.

chapters.title: Week 6: Network security
chapters.summary: Firewalls and how to configure your personal firewall, virtual private networks and their risks, the TOR browser, intrusion detection systems and honeypots.

blocks.title: Introduction to Week 6
blocks.note: Cory Doctorow notes that you are six weeks into the course. Computer networks provide the basic infrastructure for the internet and the web, so it's important to understand how they can be protected from attack. Building on networking and cryptography, this week shows how to protect the underlying networks and computers you use. Just as locking your front door protects your valuables and personal space in the real world, you'll see how to do the same for your digital life.

blocks.text: Earlier in the course you looked at a range of security techniques and technologies aimed at protecting your online identity, and your digital information, from malware.
This week explores different ways of protecting the underlying communication networks and computers we use from attack - and you'll configure a firewall for the computers you use.
By the end of this week you should be able to:

items: understand the role of firewalls in protecting networks
configure your own personal firewall on your computer
explain how cryptography enables virtual private networks (VPNs) to maintain your confidentiality, and the risks VPNs bring
describe how networks can be automatically monitored to detect attacks as they occur

blocks.alt: A building on fire with a firefighter looking on
blocks.caption: Figure 1 A firewall stops a fire - or an attack - from spreading

blocks.text: In a building, a firewall is a reinforced masonry wall designed to stop a fire spreading through the structure, giving people time to escape.

blocks.title: Firewall
blocks.text: In a computer network, a barrier that blocks dangerous communications from spreading across a network - either from the outside world into a local network, or from one part of a local network to another.
Firewalls can be dedicated network devices, part of a network router, or included in a computer's operating system.
The internet existed long before firewalls. The technologies were first discussed in late 1988, after several attacks by organised groups of hackers and the very first malicious software.

At their simplest, firewalls look at the addressing (usually IP) and protocol (usually TCP or UDP) information in each data packet's (datagram's) header and compare it with **rules** in the firewall's software. Rules may come from the manufacturer, but more often are created by an administrator or sometimes the user.

So if a packet from a hacker scanning your network arrives, the firewall checks it against its rules. If the rules say packets from an unknown address are blocked, the firewall either discards the packet 'silently' or 'closes' the connection with the hacker.

Most firewalls store the **state** of connections to tell whether packets belong to new or existing connections. They only let through packets belonging to a known, active connection (if the rules allow it).

More advanced firewalls can identify the **applications** sending and receiving packets. Network managers can then block applications that use excessive bandwidth (such as media players) or are widely used for distributing copyright-infringing content (such as BitTorrent), as well as protect against application attacks.

blocks.q: What does a simple firewall examine to decide whether to block a packet?
options: The text of the message inside the packet
The addressing and protocol information in the packet's header
The user's password
The size of the user's hard disk
blocks.explain: Simple firewalls compare the header's addressing (IP) and protocol (TCP/UDP) information against their rules.

blocks.alt: A hand with a trowel laying bricks to start building a wall
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Building your own wall

blocks.text: Most operating systems include a firewall. It protects only the computer it is installed on (and devices attached to it), so it is called a **personal firewall**. It does not replace a network firewall, which prevents attacks from outside the network (such as the internet).

Personal firewalls are especially useful on portable computers that connect to many networks. We hope those networks are safely run, but can't be sure they aren't compromised - a personal firewall adds a layer of protection between our data and a potentially untrustworthy (but useful) network.
They are the responsibility of individual users: with full access to your settings you can turn the firewall off and leave your computer vulnerable.

pages.title: How well protected are you now?

blocks.text: You can check your computer by visiting a site that probes it to see what it can access and what is blocked: **grc.com/shieldsup**. Read the information on that page first. The results you want to see:

items: **Instant UPnP Exposure test**: 'The equipment at the target IP address did not respond to our UPnP probes!'
**File sharing probe**: 'Your Internet port 139 does not appear to exist! One or more ports on this system are operating in FULL STEALTH MODE! Unable to connect with NetBIOS to your computer.'
**Common ports**: a green 'Stealth' status for all ports.
**All service ports**: a complete green 'Stealth' grid.
**Messenger spam**: the course author has it turned off.

blocks.title: Probe your own computer
blocks.prompt: Run the ShieldsUP tests on a computer you use. Note which results matched the 'good' responses and which did not. What do the results tell you about your firewall? (After updating your firewall in the next sections, run the probes again.)
blocks.hint: Look for 'Stealth' results and for ports reported as open or closed rather than stealthed.
blocks.model: Most of my common ports showed green 'Stealth', meaning my firewall did not respond to the probes so my computer is hard to find. The UPnP probe got no response, which is good. One port showed as 'closed' rather than stealth, so my computer revealed it exists - I'll check my firewall settings and re-run the test afterwards.
points: Stealth means the computer does not respond to probes
Open ports are possible routes in for attackers
UPnP and file sharing (port 139) should not respond
Re-test after changing firewall settings

blocks.text: Now locate the personal firewall on your computer and, if necessary, change its settings to give the best possible protection.

blocks.title: Before you start
blocks.text: You need Administrator access because you'll change important parts of the operating system - ask the owner for temporary rights if needed. On an office or employer-supplied computer, check you are allowed to change firewall settings: many employers have preferred settings maintained by specialist staff.

items: **Windows 10**: the firewall should be on by default; Microsoft's support page explains how to check it is turned on.
**Apple**: Apple takes responsibility for the security functions of its devices and publishes security guidance.
**Linux**: you have a lot of choice about which firewall to run (e.g. iptables, firewalld).

blocks.title: Configuring your own firewall (PC)
blocks.note: On Windows 7: Start menu > Control Panel > System and Security > Windows Firewall > Turn Windows Firewall On or Off (you may need an administrator password). If it isn't active, turn it on for each network type your computer supports. Most applications are blocked when it is first activated; tick 'Notify me when Windows Firewall blocks a new app' so Windows asks permission whenever an app first tries to connect - only allow apps you're sure are safe; your choice is remembered. For maximum protection choose 'Block all incoming connections, including those in the list of allowed apps', which stops other computers connecting unless your computer requested the data - very useful when travelling and using public wi-fi.

blocks.text: A downloadable PDF of these instructions (Windows 7) was provided by the course to keep as a reference. You can skip the Mac part unless you also own a Mac.

blocks.title: Configuring your own firewall (Mac)
blocks.note: Open System Preferences > Security and Privacy > Firewall tab. If needed, click the padlock icon, enter your password and click Turn On Firewall. Firewall Options: 'Block all incoming connections' stops traffic from external computers other than some basic network services. The list shows programs allowed to send and receive data; add software with the + button. 'Automatically allow signed software to receive incoming connections' lets digitally signed applications communicate. 'Stealth Mode' stops your computer responding to ping messages that attackers sometimes use to find targets. Confirm changes with OK.

blocks.text: Apple's support pages explain the application firewall and how to change Firewall preferences on a Mac; the course also provided a PDF of these instructions.

blocks.q: Stealth Mode stops your computer replying to ping messages that attackers use to identify potential targets.
blocks.explain: That is exactly what the Mac's Stealth Mode option does.

blocks.text: Other firewalls can be downloaded or bought. Make sure any software you download has been fully evaluated by organisations with the expertise to do so - apps found via a search engine or an Android app store may contain malware. If you use one, remember:

items: keep only **one** firewall running at a time - several don't offer significantly better protection and can interfere with one another
you must keep one firewall running **at all times**

blocks.title: Allow or deny?
blocks.prompt: Once you've set up your personal firewall, identify a type of traffic that you might want to allow (or deny) on your computer, and explain why.
blocks.model: I would deny all incoming connections when using public wi-fi in a cafe, so other computers on that network can't connect to my laptop unless I requested the data. At home I might allow a specific trusted application, such as my video-call software, to receive incoming connections, because I know where it came from and need it to work.
points: Name a specific type of traffic or application
Say whether to allow or deny it
Justify the choice by risk, e.g. untrusted public networks
Only allow applications you are sure are safe

blocks.alt: Black-and-white Wild West film scene of two gunmen shooting at each other in a street
blocks.caption: Figure 3 The lawless frontier

blocks.text: Our local networks resemble forts in a Hollywood Wild West: inside strong walls data is exchanged freely between trusted machines; beyond the firewall lies the lawless frontier of the internet, where traffic makes a risky, largely unprotected journey.

This is especially acute for organisations on several sites, those working with sub-contractors, and those with dispersed workforces such as sales teams or home workers. Traditionally they used private **leased lines** costing thousands of pounds a month - too expensive for most, and no use for a mobile workforce. So the internet is our only choice - and this is where VPNs come to the rescue.

blocks.title: Virtual private network (VPN)
blocks.text: A means of creating a private network across an untrusted network such as the internet.
VPNs can be used:

items: to securely connect isolated local area networks (LANs) across the internet
to allow mobile users remote access to a corporate network using the internet
to control access within an intranet environment

blocks.q: Leased lines are the cheaper alternative to VPNs for a mobile, dispersed workforce.
blocks.explain: Leased lines can cost thousands of pounds a month and cannot serve a mobile or highly dispersed workforce - VPNs use the internet instead.

blocks.text: VPNs typically use dedicated network devices (sometimes a firewall) and software in two parts:

items: **VPN client** - installed on the computer of anyone who wants to join the VPN; it connects the user so they can send and receive information securely with, for example, the corporate network.
**VPN server** - part of a dedicated device, usually on the perimeter of the organisation's network; it typically authenticates users and routes traffic to the corporate network.

blocks.text: The software creates a path called a **tunnel** between client and server across any untrusted network such as the internet. Information in the tunnel can be encrypted to protect it from inspection or modification - protecting our data as it crosses the lawless frontier back to the safety of our forts.

pages.title: VPNs on open networks and at home

blocks.text: VPN for an open network

Public wi-fi in cafes, hotels and airports can let your data be intercepted and your movements tracked, and some countries monitor all internet traffic. A VPN service provides a client for your computer and servers at safe locations worldwide acting as gateways onto the internet. An encrypted tunnel connects you to the remote server, so to the outside world your computer appears to be at the VPN exit point, perhaps in another country.
Free VPN services exist but tend to be slow. If personal security matters, use a service that doesn't log user data in any way - ProtonVPN is an example.
VPN for a personal private network

You can run VPN server software on your home computer. A VPN client on your mobile device connects to it through an encrypted tunnel, giving you secure access to your home computer from anywhere. To the outside internet you appear to be browsing from home.

blocks.alt: Abstract image of a bright pink tunnel lined with photographs
blocks.caption: Figure 4 The VPN tunnel

blocks.text: **Encryption**: the tunnel relies on encryption to protect data from interception or modification. It is usually done by the client and server software. Early VPNs used proprietary encryption, but shortcomings forced a switch to public encryption standards.

**Authenticity and integrity**: information must come from an authenticated user and not be altered in transit. VPNs use **hashes** and **digital signatures** (Week 5) and **message authentication codes (MACs)**. MACs are appended to messages as an authenticator - similar to digital signatures, but the hash is encrypted and decrypted with the same secret key (symmetric encryption).

blocks.q: How does a message authentication code (MAC) differ from a digital signature?
options: A MAC hides the message contents
A MAC encrypts and decrypts the hash with the same secret key
A MAC needs a Certificate Authority
A MAC uses no hash at all
blocks.explain: A MAC works like a signature but uses symmetric encryption - one shared secret key - rather than a private/public key pair.

items: **PPTP (Point to Point Tunnelling Protocol)** - designed by a Microsoft-led consortium; standard in Windows NT 4 and a free add-on for Windows 95/98. Unsuited to large companies (255 connections per server) and, worse, it didn't settle on one form of authentication or encryption, so different PPTP products could be incompatible. Replaced by L2TP from Windows 2000.
**L2TP (Layer 2 Tunnelling Protocol)** - an adaptation of Cisco's L2F (built to compete with PPTP), devised by the PPTP Forum, Cisco and the IETF; combines features of PPTP and L2F.

**IPSec (Internet Protocol Security)** - designed by the IETF from 1992 (draft 1995, revised 1998). Now the most widely supported, backed by Intel, IBM, HP/Compaq and Microsoft. Trusted because it builds on existing, intensely scrutinised encryption technologies rather than inventing new ones.
**OpenVPN** - an open source VPN developed in 2004, based on SSL/TLS, designed to be simpler to set up and operate.

blocks.title: Match each description to the VPN protocol

pairs.def: Microsoft-led design limited to 255 connections per server, with no single agreed authentication or encryption
Combines features of PPTP and Cisco's L2F; replaced PPTP from Windows 2000
IETF design, now the most widely supported, built on well-scrutinised existing encryption
Open source VPN from 2004 based on SSL/TLS, designed to be simpler to set up

pages.title: 2.2 Security risks of VPN: remote machines

blocks.alt: An open laptop on a beach with the sea and mountains behind
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Working from anywhere extends the network

blocks.text: VPNs may sound like a panacea, extending a corporate network across a wide area via the internet - but they raise new problems.

A remote machine on a VPN creates a new frontier between the 'secure' corporate network and the internet - a direct route in. The remote user may use their own computer, connection, operating system and software, none controlled by the organisation, and may share the machine with others - perhaps managing corporate documents, downloading pirated music and playing games on the same PC!

Remote machines must be secured: enforce minimum standards for operating system, antivirus and firewalls, require up-to-date antivirus and all patches, and consider severely limiting what remote users can access.

items: **Implementation** - a well-designed protocol can be undermined by programmers' shortcuts or 'additional convenience'. There were no major problems with the PPTP protocol, but Microsoft's 1996 implementation had serious defects; hacker tools exploited them the next year, papers appeared in 1998, and only then did Microsoft patch the worst (DUN 1.3) - some issues remained. Poor design or configuration of the overall VPN can also introduce vulnerabilities.
**Interoperation** - competing standards from different vendors; mixing hardware and software may cause problems, so until the technology matures a single provider may be needed.
**Network availability** - VPNs rely on the internet, which cannot guarantee delivery, so reliability isn't guaranteed.

blocks.q: The PPTP example shows that a VPN can be insecure even when...
options: the remote user's computer is fully patched
the protocol itself is well designed, because the implementation is flawed
the internet is reliable
only one vendor is used
blocks.explain: The PPTP protocol had no major problems, but Microsoft's implementation of it had serious defects.

blocks.alt: A smiling man working on a laptop at a desk
blocks.caption: Figure 6 VPNs have many real-world applications

blocks.title: Activity 1 VPN applications (about 30 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Find out about some VPN applications (services and software). What are the potential security problems associated with some of them? Note down your thoughts.
blocks.hint: Starting points suggested by the course: reviews of the best and most secure VPN services (PCMag, TechRadar), reasons to use OpenVPN, and the 'Five Eyes' intelligence-sharing concept (vpnmentor), plus the OpenVPN overview.
blocks.model: VPN services differ greatly. Some free services are slow or may log and sell user data, which defeats the purpose; a provider that keeps no logs is safer. Where the provider is based matters, because some countries (such as those in the 'Five Eyes' alliance) may require providers to share data. Older protocols like PPTP are weak, so services using OpenVPN or IPSec are preferable. Remember the VPN provider can see your traffic, so you must trust it.
points: Some VPN providers log user data
Free services may be slow or less trustworthy
Provider's country and laws (e.g. Five Eyes) matter
Protocol choice matters: PPTP weak, OpenVPN/IPSec stronger
You must trust the VPN provider with your traffic

blocks.text: The TOR Browser is designed to maximise security against attacks on communications between the user and the wider internet. TOR stands for **The Onion Router**: the user's traffic is encrypted and routed through three random TOR relays anywhere in the world, changed every few minutes. The third relay sends the traffic on as normal HTTPS without revealing the original source.

Over public wi-fi, an attacker can detect that you're using TOR - but that is all. Random public wi-fi plus the TOR browser is one of the safest ways for a journalist to communicate in a hostile environment. Using TOR to access ProtonMail hides even the fact that you use ProtonMail.

items: only download the TOR browser from torproject.org
don't add any 'addons' - they may break the security
don't use a VPN as well as TOR - this may also break some aspects of security

blocks.q: For extra safety you should run a VPN at the same time as the TOR browser.
blocks.explain: The course advises not to use a VPN as well as TOR, as this may break some aspects of security.

blocks.alt: Close-up of green plastic toy soldiers
blocks.caption: Figure 7 Defending against attack

blocks.text: In films, a network attack means frantic typing, flashing lights and sirens. In real life networks are regularly attacked, but the response is rarely that exciting.
Intrusion detection systems may be a dedicated device or software, of two types:

items: **Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS)** - monitors data passing over a network.
**Host Intrusion Detection System (HIDS)** - monitors data to and from a computer.

blocks.text: An IDS supports a network firewall. Ideally the firewall is closed to all traffic except what the organisation needs (such as web, email and FTP). A NIDS scans traffic passing through the firewall for attacks, and a HIDS detects attacks from within - such as a PC infected with malware.

Intrusion detection can be **passive**: it identifies an intrusion and informs an administrator, who must act. It can also be **reactive**: it informs the administrator and actively tries to stop the intrusion, usually by blocking further packets from the source IP address. These are also called an **Intrusion Prevention (or Protection) System (IPS)**.
Weaknesses

items: too sensitive - falsely reporting an intrusion, e.g. if a network is misconfigured or a buggy program issues large numbers of packets
not sensitive enough - to attacks that proceed very slowly and generate too little traffic to raise the alarm
signature IDS depends on suppliers issuing regular updates; until the update arrives, it is effectively blind to the attack

blocks.q: An IDS that automatically blocks further packets from an attacker's IP address is known as...
options: a honeypot
an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)
a passive IDS
a VPN server
blocks.explain: A reactive IDS that actively tries to stop intrusions is also called an Intrusion Prevention or Protection System.

blocks.alt: Close-up of four warning lights in red and blue
blocks.caption: Figure 8 Raising the alarm

blocks.text: Intrusion detection typically uses **anomaly detection** or **misuse detection**.

Anomaly detection depends on a model of expected 'normal' behaviour of users and applications, assuming attacks differ from normal behaviour. Its advantage: it can detect previously unknown attacks by spotting deviations.

Example: a user normally logs on at 9am each weekday, uses an order processing application in the morning, visits supplier websites in the afternoon and logs off at 5pm. If the system logs him accessing it at 3am and installing new software, this is flagged as suspicious. The disadvantage: some legitimate activities may be wrongly flagged.

Misuse detection depends on a set of attack patterns, or **signatures**, configured by an administrator together with patterns of normal behaviour. When users' activity matches an attack signature, or mis-matches a configured normal-use pattern, the system flags an attack.

blocks.q: A brand-new attack with no known pattern is most likely to be caught by which technique?
options: Misuse detection
Anomaly detection
Neither can ever detect it
A personal firewall's Stealth Mode
blocks.explain: Anomaly detection looks for deviations from normal behaviour, so it can detect previously unknown attacks; misuse detection only recognises known signatures.

blocks.alt: An old desktop computer sitting on a mousetrap
blocks.caption: Figure 9 A honeypot is a trap

blocks.text: Network administrators sometimes want to study attacks - to understand attackers' methods and prepare countermeasures, or as part of an investigation that might lead to civil or criminal prosecution.

blocks.title: Honeypot
blocks.text: An isolated computer or network that appears completely legitimate but is in fact a closely monitored trap. Attackers are deflected towards it, and every action they perform can be recorded and analysed without risking important data.
Honeypots are also used by researchers to identify new attacks circulating in the hacking community, and by anti-spam organisations to identify the location and identities of spam senders.

blocks.q: A honeypot holds an organisation's most important data to lure attackers.
blocks.explain: A honeypot is isolated and only appears legitimate, so attackers can be studied without risking important data.

cards.back: A barrier that blocks dangerous communications from spreading across a network
A firewall in the operating system that protects only the computer it is installed on
A means of creating a private network across an untrusted network such as the internet
The (usually encrypted) path a VPN creates between the VPN client and VPN server
Message authentication code: a hash encrypted with a shared secret key, appended to a message as an authenticator
Network IDS monitors data on a network; Host IDS monitors data to and from a computer
Intrusion Prevention System: a reactive IDS that also tries to stop the intrusion
A closely monitored trap system that looks legitimate, used to study attackers

blocks.q: Why are personal firewalls especially useful on portable computers?
options: They make the computer faster
Laptops connect to many networks that may be compromised
They replace the need for a network firewall
They encrypt all web traffic
blocks.explain: A personal firewall adds a layer of protection between your data and potentially untrustworthy networks; it does not replace a network firewall.

blocks.q: Which is the course's advice on running firewalls?
options: Run as many firewalls as possible
Run one firewall at all times - no more, no fewer
Turn the firewall off on public wi-fi
Firewalls are only needed on desktop PCs
blocks.explain: Multiple firewalls don't add much and can interfere with each other, but one must be running at all times.

blocks.q: Which VPN protocol is now the most widely supported?
options: PPTP
L2F
IPSec
DES
blocks.explain: IPSec, designed by the IETF, is the most widely supported, backed by Intel, IBM, HP/Compaq and Microsoft.

blocks.q: Which of these are security risks introduced by VPNs?
options: Remote machines the organisation doesn't control
Flawed implementations of protocols
Guaranteed delivery over the internet
Incompatibility between vendors' products
blocks.explain: Remote machines, implementation flaws and interoperation problems are all risks. The internet cannot guarantee delivery - availability is another risk.

blocks.q: How does TOR hide where your traffic comes from?
options: It routes encrypted traffic through three random relays that change every few minutes
It uses a leased line
It turns off your firewall
It deletes your DNS records
blocks.explain: The Onion Router encrypts traffic and passes it through three random relays; the last sends it on as normal HTTPS without revealing the source.

blocks.q: Which weakness applies to a signature-based IDS?
options: It can only monitor one computer
It is blind to attacks until it receives updated signatures
It needs a honeypot to work
It cannot be used with a firewall
blocks.explain: Signature IDS relies on suppliers issuing regular updates; until then it is effectively blind to the new attack.

blocks.caption: Figure 10 Network-level protection for your digital life

blocks.text: This week focused on techniques for network-level protection of your digital life. You learned the role of firewalls in protecting networks and configured a personal firewall for the computers you use. You also learned how cryptography maintains the confidentiality, integrity and authenticity of network traffic in VPNs, and how networks can be automatically monitored to detect potential attacks.
Next: Week 7: When your defences fail.
