blocks.text: Answers right first time earn more marks than on a second or third attempt. See the badge as an opportunity to reflect on what you have learned rather than as a test - read each explanation after you answer.

blocks.q: Under the CIA principles, which was violated when unauthorised people read Equifax's customer records (while the data stayed available and unchanged)?
options: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
blocks.explain: Confidentiality means information is read only by the right people. Authorised users still had access (availability) and the data was not changed (integrity).

blocks.q: What is 'salting' a password?
options: Storing the password in plaintext on a separate server
Adding a random value to the plaintext password before it is hashed
Asking the user to change their password every month
blocks.explain: Salting means that even identical passwords produce completely different hashes; it only works if salts are truly random and long enough.

blocks.q: Withdrawing cash from an ATM with your bank card and PIN is an example of two-factor authentication.
blocks.explain: Neither the card data nor the PIN alone can access your account; together they can.

blocks.q: How does a worm differ from a virus?
options: A worm is a standalone application that spreads itself through network connections
A worm cannot make copies of itself
A worm disguises itself as a legitimate program such as a screensaver
blocks.explain: Both self-replicate, but a worm is standalone and spreads over networks. The third option describes a Trojan.

blocks.q: Trojans are self-replicating: they copy themselves to other computers without any help from users.
blocks.explain: Unlike viruses and worms, Trojans are not self-replicating - they rely on their apparent usefulness to spread.

blocks.q: In a botnet, what is a 'zombie'?
options: The control computer that sends instructions
An infected computer that waits, apparently doing nothing, for instructions from the control computer
An antivirus program that has stopped updating
blocks.explain: Zombies periodically check for instructions, so they don't raise suspicion until the botnet is used - e.g. for spam or denial-of-service attacks.

blocks.q: What is a firewall in a computer network?
options: A barrier that blocks dangerous communications spreading into a local network or between parts of it
A program that encrypts all files on a disk
A backup copy stored in a fireproof building
blocks.explain: Like a building's firewall stops fire spreading, a network firewall blocks dangerous communications. It can be a device, part of a router or part of the operating system.

blocks.q: Traditionally, what was the 'enormous shortcoming' of symmetric encryption?
options: It could not encrypt long messages
The key had to be sent to the other party, and could be stolen or copied in transit
Messages could only be decrypted by the sender
blocks.explain: Whoever intercepted the key could decrypt any ciphertext encrypted with it - and many key pairs are needed between communicating parties.

blocks.q: Which intrusion detection technique can spot previously unknown attacks, but may flag some legitimate activity as suspicious?
options: Misuse detection
Anomaly detection
A honeypot
blocks.explain: Anomaly detection compares activity with a model of normal behaviour. Misuse detection uses known attack signatures, so it misses new patterns; a honeypot is a monitored trap for studying attackers.

blocks.q: A hacker exploits an unpatched vulnerability to steal a customer database. Under which UK law has the hacker committed an offence?
options: Data Protection Act
Computer Misuse Act
Fraud Act
RIPA
blocks.explain: Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system is a CMA offence. The organisation, for failing to patch, would have breached the DPA.

blocks.q: Most cloud storage services are synchronised, so deleting a file on your computer usually deletes the cloud copy too.
blocks.explain: That's why cloud sync alone doesn't protect you against deletion - although some services keep previous versions.

blocks.q: Which is the best way to guarantee your data is safe once it is stored in the cloud?
options: Trust the provider's security policy
Encrypt the contents, e.g. in encrypted folders inside your cloud folder
Encrypt your whole hard drive
blocks.explain: Encryption is the only guarantee. Whole-drive encryption does not encrypt the files you back up from the drive.

blocks.q: Lewis's study materials and digital photographs belong in which box of the risk grid?
options: High impact, high likelihood
High impact, low likelihood
Low impact, high likelihood
Low impact, low likelihood
blocks.explain: Losing them would hurt, but they have minimal financial value to an attacker, so an attack is unlikely.

blocks.q: Taking out insurance to cover losses if a threat materialises is an example of...
options: avoiding the risk
modifying the risk
transferring the risk
accepting the risk
blocks.explain: Transferring passes the cost of the risk to others, typically an insurer.

blocks.q: Which of these are on the course's 'do the basics' checklist? Select all that apply.
options: Use a unique strong password for each website
Set up two-factor authentication for important financial and social media sites
Use the administrator account for everyday web browsing
Get used to making backups
blocks.explain: Never browse the web or open emails using an administrator account - use a standard account day to day.
